D: A
T: How do JSON columns work in EF Core and SQL Server?
K: json columns ef core, tojson, store json in sql server, openjson, json_value, owned types json
X: EF Core 7 and later can map an owned type, or a collection of owned types, to a single JSON column, using ToJson in the configuration. For example, a Study entity could store its flexible settings, or a shipment its list of temperature readings, as JSON, while the rest of the entity stays in normal columns.
X: The nice part is that queries still work in LINQ. EF translates filters on JSON properties into SQL Server's JSON functions, like JSON_VALUE and OPENJSON, so I can write Where s.Settings.MaxKits greater than 10, and it becomes SQL. Updates can modify just part of the JSON. EF Core 8 added primitive collections, like a List of int stored as JSON, and SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL now have a native json data type, which is more efficient than nvarchar.
X: When is it a good fit? For data that's naturally a document, owned by one entity and usually read together with it: flexible attributes that vary by study or customer, configuration blobs, or small nested lists. It avoids lots of small tables and joins.
X: When is it a bad fit? For data that needs relational integrity, foreign keys, frequent filtering and sorting, or joins with other tables. Filtering on JSON properties can't use normal indexes unless I add computed columns with indexes on the extracted values.
X: So I use it selectively, not as a way to avoid designing a schema.
@p17-232
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is DbContext pooling, and when does it help?
K: dbcontext pooling, adddbcontextpool, context pooling performance, pooled dbcontext factory
X: Normally, ASP.NET Core creates a new DbContext instance for each request and disposes it at the end. Creating a DbContext is fairly cheap, but in very high-throughput services, the setup work, like initialising internal services and the change tracker, adds up.
X: With AddDbContextPool instead of AddDbContext, EF Core keeps a pool of DbContext instances. When a request needs one, it takes one from the pool; at the end, the context is reset, clearing tracked entities and state, and returned to the pool for the next request. That reduces allocation and setup overhead. AddPooledDbContextFactory does the same for code that creates contexts through a factory, like background services or Blazor.
X: Benchmarks show measurable gains only for very high request rates with simple queries, so for many apps it's a minor optimisation. It's worth turning on when profiling shows context creation in the hot path.
X: The important limitation: because instances are reused, the DbContext must not hold per-request state in its own fields, like a tenant id or current user injected through the constructor, since a pooled instance could carry one request's state into another. Constructor injection of scoped services into a pooled DbContext doesn't work as usual. For multi-tenant scenarios, I set the per-request state after getting the context from the pool, using a factory or a custom approach that resets it.
X: Note this is different from database connection pooling, which ADO.NET does anyway.
@p17-233
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is connection pool exhaustion, and how do you fix it?
K: connection pool exhaustion, timeout expired max pool size, connection leak, sqlconnection pool, max pool size reached
X: ADO.NET keeps a pool of open database connections per connection string, 100 by default. When code opens a connection, it gets one from the pool, and closing or disposing it returns it to the pool. If all connections are in use, the next request waits, and after the timeout, it fails with an error like "Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool. This may have occurred because all pooled connections were in use and max pool size was reached."
X: The common causes. Connection leaks: code that opens connections or data readers without disposing them, especially when an exception skips the close, so connections are never returned. Long-running queries or transactions holding connections for a long time. Sync-over-async or thread pool starvation, where connections are held while threads wait. A traffic spike with slow database responses, so more requests hold connections at once. And slightly different connection strings creating separate pools.
X: To diagnose, I check the number of connections from the app's host in sys.dm_exec_sessions, look at what those sessions are doing, and review code for missing using statements or DbContexts not disposed. EF Core and DI handle disposal correctly if contexts are scoped properly.
X: The fixes are disposing connections with using, shorter transactions, faster queries, and async code all the way. Increasing Max Pool Size only hides the problem, and can overload the database.
@p17-234
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Dapper vs EF Core: when do you use each?
K: dapper vs ef core, micro orm, dapper performance, use both dapper and ef, raw sql vs orm
X: Dapper is a micro-ORM: I write the SQL myself, and Dapper maps results to objects and handles parameters. It's very fast, with almost no overhead over raw ADO.NET, and gives complete control over the SQL.
X: EF Core is a full ORM: LINQ queries translated to SQL, change tracking, relationships, migrations, concurrency handling, interceptors and much more. Developers are productive, and the code is strongly typed and refactor-friendly.
X: The performance gap has narrowed a lot in recent versions. EF Core with AsNoTracking and projections to DTOs is close to Dapper for most queries, so performance alone rarely decides it.
X: I use EF Core for most application code, especially writes, where change tracking, validation of relationships, concurrency tokens and transactions save a lot of code and mistakes, and for typical queries.
X: I use Dapper, or EF Core's raw SQL features like SqlQuery, when I need hand-tuned SQL: complex reporting queries with window functions or CTEs, queries against legacy stored procedures, bulk reads where every millisecond counts, or databases that EF doesn't model well.
X: Using both in the same service is completely fine, even sharing the same connection and transaction.
X: In our CIRT platform, the newer APIs use EF Core, while the legacy parts rely heavily on stored procedures with ADO.NET-style data access.
@p17-235
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is EF Core's execution strategy, and how does it work with transactions?
K: execution strategy ef core, enableretryonfailure, retry transient sql errors, user initiated transactions not supported, sql azure transient
X: EnableRetryOnFailure turns on EF Core's retrying execution strategy for SQL Server. When a command fails with a transient error, like a brief network drop, a failover, or Azure SQL throttling, EF Core waits and retries automatically, with an increasing delay, up to a maximum number of attempts. That makes the app much more resilient in cloud environments, where short blips are normal.
X: The catch is transactions. If I start a transaction myself, with BeginTransaction, and a command fails in the middle, EF can't just retry that one command, because the earlier work in the transaction was rolled back. So EF Core throws an error saying user-initiated transactions aren't supported with the retrying strategy.
X: The fix is to wrap the whole unit of work in the strategy: get it with context.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy, and call ExecuteAsync with a delegate that begins the transaction, does all the work, saves and commits. If a transient failure happens, the strategy re-runs the entire delegate from the start, including beginning a new transaction.
X: That means the delegate must be safe to repeat. It should reload any data it depends on, rather than reusing state from the failed attempt, and avoid side effects outside the database, like sending an email, inside the retried block.
X: There's also a subtle case where the commit succeeded but the connection failed before confirming it. Making operations idempotent, or using verifySucceeded, protects against applying it twice.
@p17-236
S: sqlx
D: A
T: char vs varchar vs nvarchar: how do you choose?
K: char vs varchar, varchar vs nvarchar, unicode columns, utf8 collation, column data type choice, nvarchar max
X: char is fixed-length: char(10) always uses 10 bytes, padding shorter values with spaces. It's good for values that are always the same length, like a two-letter country code or a fixed-format code.
X: varchar is variable-length, using only the bytes needed plus two bytes of overhead, so it's better for values of varying length, like names or descriptions.
X: nvarchar and nchar store Unicode, traditionally UTF-16, using two bytes per character for most text. They can store any language: Japanese, Arabic, Hindi, accented names. varchar uses a code page, so characters outside it get lost or become question marks, unless the column uses a UTF-8 collation, available since SQL Server 2019, which lets varchar store Unicode as UTF-8.
X: So for any text that users type, like names, addresses or comments, especially in a global system, I use nvarchar, or varchar with a UTF-8 collation. For internal codes and identifiers that are guaranteed ASCII, varchar saves space.
X: Other practices. Size columns realistically, not nvarchar(max) everywhere. Max types are stored differently, can't be index keys, and the declared size affects the memory grants the optimiser requests. And match the parameter types from the application to the column types, because a mismatch, like nvarchar parameters against a varchar column, can cause implicit conversions and index scans.
@p17-237
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do NULLs behave in SQL, and what is COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
K: null in sql, count star vs count column, null comparison, is null, ansi nulls, coalesce isnull
X: NULL means unknown or missing, not zero and not empty string, and it follows three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL return unknown, not true or false.
X: That leads to classic surprises. WHERE Column equals NULL returns nothing; I must use IS NULL. WHERE Status not equals 'Shipped' excludes rows where Status is NULL, because NULL not equals 'Shipped' is unknown. NOT IN with a subquery that returns any NULL returns no rows at all, which is a nasty bug; NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem.
X: COUNT of star counts all rows. COUNT of a column counts only rows where that column isn't NULL. COUNT DISTINCT also ignores NULLs. Aggregates like SUM and AVG ignore NULLs, so AVG of a column with NULLs isn't the same as SUM divided by COUNT star. And SUM of all NULLs returns NULL, not zero, so I wrap it in COALESCE.
X: For defaults, COALESCE is standard SQL and accepts many arguments, while ISNULL is SQL Server-specific, takes two, and uses the first argument's data type, which can truncate values.
X: NULLs in unique constraints: SQL Server allows only one NULL in a unique column, unlike some databases, so a filtered unique index is used to allow many.
X: In design, I make columns NOT NULL unless missing values are genuinely meaningful.
@p17-238
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
K: where vs having, having clause, filter aggregates, group by having, logical query processing order
X: WHERE filters individual rows before they're grouped. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. So conditions on raw columns go in WHERE, and conditions on aggregates, like COUNT, SUM or AVG, go in HAVING.
X: For example, to find sites with more than 50 dispensed kits this year: WHERE DispenseDate is in this year and Status equals Dispensed limits the rows first, then GROUP BY SiteId, then HAVING COUNT of star greater than 50 keeps only the groups with enough kits.
X: This follows the logical processing order of a query: FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, and finally TOP or OFFSET. That order also explains why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE, because SELECT hasn't happened yet, but you can use it in ORDER BY.
X: For performance, I put row conditions in WHERE whenever possible, not in HAVING, so fewer rows are grouped. The optimiser can often move simple HAVING conditions on grouping columns into WHERE, but writing it correctly makes intent clear and doesn't depend on that.
X: It's a basic question, but I've seen real bugs where a condition was put in HAVING on a non-aggregated column, or a filter on an outer-joined table in WHERE turned a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.
@p17-239
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you write an upsert, and what are the risks of MERGE?
K: upsert sql server, merge statement, insert or update, merge race condition, update then insert pattern
X: An upsert updates a row if it exists, or inserts it if it doesn't. It's very common when syncing data from external systems, like vendor shipment statuses.
X: SQL Server's MERGE statement can do it in one statement: MERGE into the target, USING the source, ON the key, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, and optionally WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE. It's powerful for syncing a whole set of rows from a staging table.
X: But MERGE has a reputation for problems. It isn't safe under concurrency by default: two sessions can both see that a row doesn't exist and both try to insert, causing primary key violations, unless I add a HOLDLOCK or SERIALIZABLE hint. It has had a number of bugs over the years, especially with filtered indexes, triggers and certain features. And it's easy to write in a way that does something unexpected.
X: For single-row upserts, many SQL Server developers prefer an explicit pattern inside a transaction: UPDATE with UPDLOCK and SERIALIZABLE hints, and if no rows were affected, INSERT. The lock hints prevent the race. For sets of rows, an UPDATE joined to the staging table followed by an INSERT of rows that don't exist, in one transaction.
X: In EF Core, there's no built-in upsert yet, so for high volumes I use SQL directly or a library.
@p17-240
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Cursors vs set-based queries: why avoid cursors?
K: cursor vs set based, sql cursor performance, row by row processing, rbar, while loop sql
X: SQL Server is designed for set-based operations: describing what result you want for a whole set of rows in one statement, and letting the optimiser decide how to do it efficiently, using indexes, joins, parallelism and batching.
X: A cursor processes rows one at a time, like a loop in procedural code. Each iteration fetches a row and runs separate statements for it. People call this RBAR, "row by agonising row". For a large table, it's typically orders of magnitude slower than an equivalent set-based UPDATE or INSERT ... SELECT, because each row has its own overhead, locks are held longer, and the optimiser can't optimise the whole operation. WHILE loops that process one row at a time have the same problem.
X: So when I see a cursor, I try to rewrite it as one or a few set-based statements, using joins, CASE expressions, window functions like ROW_NUMBER or running totals with SUM OVER, and CTEs.
X: There are legitimate uses for cursors or loops. Administrative tasks that must run something per database or per object, like maintenance across many study databases. Calling a stored procedure that only works one row at a time and can't be changed. And deliberately processing in batches, which is a loop over chunks of thousands of rows, not single rows, to control locking and log growth.
X: If I must use a cursor, I declare it LOCAL FAST_FORWARD for lower overhead.
@p17-241
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you write dynamic SQL safely?
K: dynamic sql, sp_executesql, exec vs sp_executesql, dynamic search query, quotename, dynamic sql injection
X: Dynamic SQL is building a SQL statement as a string and executing it, which is sometimes necessary, like search screens with many optional filters, dynamic sorting, or administrative scripts that work across tables or databases.
X: The rules I follow. Use sp_executesql, not EXEC of a concatenated string. sp_executesql takes parameters separately, so user values are never part of the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection. It also allows plan reuse, because the SQL text is the same for different parameter values.
X: Never concatenate user input as values. Only the structure of the query is built dynamically, like adding "AND SiteId equals @SiteId" when that filter is present, and the values are always passed as parameters.
X: For identifiers, like table names, column names or sort direction, which can't be parameters, I validate them against a whitelist of allowed names, and wrap them with QUOTENAME to handle special characters safely.
X: For catch-all search queries with optional filters, building the WHERE clause dynamically with only the filters actually used often gives much better plans than one static query with "OR @Param IS NULL" conditions, which tends to produce poor, generic plans. OPTION RECOMPILE is the other alternative for those.
X: Dynamic SQL runs with the caller's permissions, and it's harder to read and review, so I keep it small, well commented, and print it in debug mode.
@p17-242
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you handle errors and transactions in T-SQL with TRY/CATCH and XACT_ABORT?
K: try catch sql server, xact_abort, t sql error handling, rollback in catch, throw vs raiserror, xact_state
X: In stored procedures that change data, I use a standard pattern so errors never leave a transaction half-done or open.
X: At the top, SET XACT_ABORT ON, and SET NOCOUNT ON. With XACT_ABORT on, most runtime errors automatically roll back the whole transaction and abort the batch. Without it, some errors only fail the current statement, and the transaction continues, which can leave partial changes. It also matters when the client times out: the transaction is rolled back instead of staying open, holding locks.
X: Then BEGIN TRY, BEGIN TRANSACTION, the statements, COMMIT TRANSACTION, END TRY. And BEGIN CATCH: if there's an open transaction, checked with @@TRANCOUNT greater than zero or XACT_STATE, ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; then log the error if needed, and rethrow it with THROW, so the application knows it failed. THROW, available since SQL Server 2012, preserves the original error number and message, and is simpler than RAISERROR.
X: Logging inside the CATCH should happen after the rollback, otherwise the log row is rolled back too.
X: Nested transactions in SQL Server aren't real nested transactions: an inner COMMIT only decrements the counter, and any ROLLBACK rolls back everything. So procedures called from other procedures should be careful about starting their own transactions, or use save points.
X: On the .NET side, I still handle SqlException and use transactions consistently.
@p17-243
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What are wait statistics, and how do you use them to tune SQL Server?
K: wait stats, sys.dm_os_wait_stats, pageiolatch, cxpacket, lck_m waits, sql server waits tuning
X: Whenever a SQL Server task can't proceed, it waits, and SQL Server records why and for how long. Wait statistics answer the question "what is the server spending its time waiting for?", which points you to the type of bottleneck before you tune anything.
X: I look at sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the server overall, filtered to exclude benign background waits, and sys.dm_exec_session_wait_stats or Query Store's wait categories for specific sessions or queries.
X: The common ones and what they suggest. PAGEIOLATCH: waiting to read data pages from disk, which suggests not enough memory for the working set, or queries reading too much data due to missing indexes. WRITELOG: waiting for transaction log writes, so slow log storage or too many tiny commits. LCK_M waits: blocking, waiting on locks held by others. CXPACKET and CXCONSUMER: parallelism, often normal, but heavy amounts may mean large scans or a cost threshold for parallelism that's too low. SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD: CPU pressure. RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE: queries waiting for memory grants, often due to big sorts or hashes from poor estimates. ASYNC_NETWORK_IO: the client isn't consuming results fast enough, often the application reading row by row or fetching huge result sets.
X: Wait stats are cumulative since restart, so I compare snapshots over a time window, during the problem period, rather than reading the totals.
@p17-244
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is tempdb contention, and how do you reduce it?
K: tempdb contention, tempdb allocation contention, pagelatch tempdb, tempdb files, tempdb spills
X: tempdb is a shared system database used by every database on the instance for temporary tables, table variables, sorts and hashes that spill out of memory, the row version store for snapshot isolation, and some internal work. Because everything shares it, it can become a bottleneck.
X: Allocation contention is the classic problem. When many sessions create and drop temporary objects at a high rate, they all compete for the same allocation pages, which show up as PAGELATCH waits on tempdb pages. Mitigations: multiple tempdb data files of equal size, usually one per CPU core up to eight, which modern SQL Server setup does by default; newer versions also reduced this contention a lot, and SQL Server 2019 added memory-optimised tempdb metadata.
X: Other tempdb problems. Spills: a sort or hash join that doesn't get enough memory writes to tempdb, which is slow, and shows as a warning in the execution plan. Fixing estimates, indexes, or the query usually helps. Version store growth: with RCSI or snapshot isolation, a long-running transaction prevents old row versions from being cleaned up, so tempdb grows. And running out of space, which can affect every database on the server.
X: So I monitor tempdb size and usage, keep it on fast storage, size it properly up front so it doesn't keep auto-growing, and look for queries with spills or excessive temporary object use.
@p17-245
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Should you blindly create every missing index suggestion that SQL Server shows in a plan?
K: missing index dmv, missing index suggestion, sys.dm_db_missing_index_details, index recommendations, database tuning advisor
X: SQL Server records missing index suggestions when the optimiser thinks an index would have helped a query. They appear in execution plans as a green hint, and in the missing index DMVs, along with an estimated improvement. They're a useful starting point, but I never create them blindly.
X: The limitations. Suggestions are made per query, without considering other indexes, so you often get several overlapping suggestions that should be combined into one. They don't consider the cost of maintaining the index on inserts and updates. The key column order isn't always ideal; equality columns are listed before inequality columns, but not ordered by selectivity. They often include many INCLUDE columns, sometimes nearly the whole table. They ignore filtered indexes and columnstore options. And the DMVs reset when the server restarts.
X: My approach: look at the suggestion together with the actual query and its execution plan, check existing indexes on the table to see if one can be extended instead of adding a new one, consider the write load on that table, design the index with the right key order and only the needed included columns, test it on a copy with realistic data, and then deploy it through the normal database change process.
X: After deploying, I verify that the query uses it and check index usage stats later, removing indexes that are never used.
@p17-246
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How does full-text search work in SQL Server, and when would you use a search engine instead?
K: full text search sql server, contains freetext, like wildcard performance, elasticsearch vs sql, search engine
X: A query with LIKE '%term%' can't use a normal index, because of the leading wildcard, so it scans the whole table, and it can't handle word forms, relevance ranking or multiple terms well.
X: SQL Server full-text search builds a special full-text index of words in text columns. Queries use CONTAINS for precise word and phrase searches, including prefix searches like "ship*", word forms through inflection, and proximity; and FREETEXT for meaning-based searching. CONTAINSTABLE and FREETEXTTABLE return relevance ranks. It handles stop words and language-specific word breaking, and the index is updated automatically in the background as data changes. Azure SQL supports it too.
X: It's a good choice when the search is part of a transactional application, the data is already in SQL Server, and requirements are moderate, like searching notes, descriptions or document text.
X: A dedicated search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, is better when search is a core feature: typo tolerance and fuzzy matching, faceted navigation, rich relevance tuning, autocomplete, searching across data from many services, very large volumes, or semantic and vector search. The cost is another system to run and keep in sync, usually through events or change data capture, with eventual consistency.
X: So I start with what the database offers, and move to a search engine when the requirements clearly need it.
@p17-247
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you manage database changes with SSDT and dacpac in a pipeline?
K: ssdt, dacpac, sql database project, sqlpackage, state based migrations, database ci cd
X: SSDT, SQL Server Data Tools, uses a declarative, state-based approach. The database project contains the desired definition of every object: tables, views, procedures, indexes, as CREATE scripts in source control. Building the project validates all the references and produces a dacpac, a package describing the target schema.
X: At deployment, SqlPackage compares the dacpac with the actual database and generates a script to make the database match: adding columns, altering procedures, creating indexes. Pre-deployment and post-deployment scripts handle data changes, like populating a new column or seeding reference data, and they must be written to be safely re-runnable.
X: In the pipeline, the build creates the dacpac as an artifact. The release first generates the deployment script, or a deploy report, for review, which is important in regulated environments, and then publishes it to each environment, with publish profiles setting options like BlockOnPossibleDataLoss, which stops the deployment if a change would drop data.
X: The advantages: the full schema is always visible in source control, drift is detected, and the same package can be deployed to many databases. The risks: automatically generated scripts can do expensive things, like rebuilding a large table to change column order, so reviewing the generated script matters.
X: Our CIRT platform uses SSDT database projects, and the same model schema is deployed to every study database.
@p17-248
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you delete or archive millions of old rows safely?
K: delete millions of rows, purge old data, archive data sql, batch delete, data retention job
X: A single DELETE of millions of rows is risky. It runs as one huge transaction, so the transaction log grows enormously, it can escalate to a table lock and block all users, it can take a very long time, and if it's cancelled, the rollback takes just as long.
X: So I do it in batches. A loop deletes, for example, 5,000 rows at a time, using DELETE TOP of 5,000 with a condition on an indexed column, like a date, and continues until no rows are affected. Each batch is its own short transaction, so locks are released quickly, below the escalation threshold, and log space can be reused between log backups. Sometimes I add a short delay between batches to reduce the impact on other users, and run it during quiet hours.
X: For archiving, each batch first copies rows to the archive table and then deletes them, in the same transaction, often using DELETE with an OUTPUT clause into the archive table, which does both in one statement.
X: For tables that are partitioned by date, switching out an old partition is almost instant, which is much better for regular retention.
X: Other points: make sure the delete condition uses an index, check for foreign keys and cascades, which can multiply the work, and consider regulatory retention rules. In clinical systems, data often must be kept for many years, so archiving is more common than deleting.
@p17-249
S: sqlx
D: A
T: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL: what are the main differences for a .NET developer?
K: sql server vs postgresql, postgres vs mssql, npgsql, postgresql for dotnet, switch to postgres
X: Both are mature, powerful relational databases, and EF Core supports both well, with Npgsql as the PostgreSQL provider.
X: Licensing and cost: PostgreSQL is open source and free, which makes it very attractive in the cloud, like RDS, Aurora PostgreSQL or Azure Database for PostgreSQL. SQL Server has licence costs, especially Enterprise edition.
X: Features where they differ. PostgreSQL has excellent JSON support with jsonb and GIN indexes, arrays as a column type, rich extensions like PostGIS and pgvector for vector search, and partial and expression indexes. SQL Server has strong tooling, like SSMS, Query Store, and SQL Server Agent for jobs, built-in columnstore, in-memory OLTP, and deep integration with Windows and Microsoft tools.
X: Behaviour differences that bite during migration. Identifiers: PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lowercase, so naming conventions matter. Case-sensitive string comparison by default in PostgreSQL. Different concurrency internals: PostgreSQL uses MVCC by default, similar to SQL Server's snapshot isolation, and needs VACUUM to clean up old row versions. Stored procedure language, T-SQL versus PL/pgSQL, so procedures must be rewritten. Data types like datetime2 versus timestamp with time zone, and identity versus serial or identity columns.
X: Our CIRT core runs on SQL Server, while the developer RAG index uses PostgreSQL with pgvector.
@p17-250
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Why should you avoid SELECT * in application queries?
K: select star, avoid select *, select all columns problem, select specific columns, projection performance
X: SELECT star returns every column of a table, and in application code, it causes several problems.
X: Performance: it reads and sends more data than needed, over the network and into memory. Wide columns, like large text or binary columns, make this much worse. It also prevents covering indexes from being used, because no non-clustered index includes every column, so SQL Server must do key lookups or scan the clustered index.
X: Fragility: if someone adds a column to the table later, the query returns it automatically. Code that relies on column order breaks, views defined with SELECT star don't pick up changes consistently until refreshed, and an INSERT ... SELECT star can fail or put data in the wrong columns.
X: Security: new sensitive columns can leak into results, logs and APIs without anyone deciding they should.
X: Readability: it's not clear which columns the code actually uses.
X: In EF Core, loading entire entities is the same thing. For read-only screens, I project with Select into a DTO with only the needed columns, which EF translates into a SELECT of just those columns, often making a big difference.
X: SELECT star is fine for ad hoc queries while exploring data, and EXISTS of SELECT star in a subquery is fine, because the columns aren't actually returned.
@p17-251
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What problems do long-running transactions cause?
K: long running transaction, open transaction problems, transaction log growth, blocking long transaction, keep transactions short
X: A transaction holds its locks until it commits or rolls back. The longer it runs, the more damage it can do.
X: Blocking: other sessions that need the locked rows, pages or tables wait, so the application slows down for many users, and deadlocks become more likely.
X: Transaction log growth: the log can't be truncated past the oldest active transaction, so a transaction left open for hours makes the log grow until the disk fills, even with regular log backups.
X: Version store growth: with snapshot isolation or RCSI, old row versions in tempdb can't be cleaned up while an old transaction might need them, so tempdb grows.
X: Recovery and rollback time: if it fails or the server restarts, rolling it back takes a long time, and the database may take longer to recover.
X: Replication and availability group lag can also increase.
X: Common causes in applications: doing slow work inside a transaction, like calling an external API, sending an email or waiting for user input; processing a huge batch in one transaction; or a bug where an exception skips the commit and the connection stays open with the transaction.
X: So I keep transactions as short as possible: prepare and validate data before starting, only include the database writes that must be atomic, do external calls outside, process large changes in batches, and monitor for old open transactions with DBCC OPENTRAN or DMVs.
@p17-252
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is a columnstore index, and when would you use one?
K: columnstore index, clustered columnstore, analytics sql server, batch mode, reporting performance, olap vs oltp
X: A normal, rowstore index stores data row by row. A columnstore index stores data column by column, in compressed segments of around a million rows.
X: That's ideal for analytics: queries that scan many rows but only a few columns, like summing quantities by site and month over millions of shipments. The query reads only the needed columns, the data is highly compressed, often 10 times smaller, and SQL Server processes it in batch mode, handling many rows per operation, which makes aggregations dramatically faster. Segment elimination also skips segments that can't match the filter.
X: There are two main uses. A clustered columnstore index makes the whole table columnar, which is right for data warehouse fact tables and large history or log tables that are mostly appended and aggregated. A non-clustered columnstore index on a transactional table enables real-time operational analytics: the OLTP workload uses the normal rowstore indexes, while reports use the columnstore, without a separate warehouse.
X: The trade-offs: they're poor for single-row lookups and frequent small updates, because updates are handled through a delta store and deleted bitmaps, and need maintenance to stay efficient.
X: So I'd consider a non-clustered columnstore for heavy reporting on a big transactional table, and clustered columnstore for warehouse or history tables. For example, aggregating supply and dispensing history for forecasting reports is a typical fit.
@p17-253
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is Change Data Capture, and how is it different from Change Tracking?
K: change data capture, cdc sql server, change tracking, debezium, stream database changes, sync data changes
X: Both are SQL Server features for finding out what changed in tables, so other systems can sync or react, without adding timestamp columns or triggers everywhere.
X: Change Tracking is lightweight. It records that a row changed, the primary key and the type of change, plus a version number, but not the old or new values. A consumer asks "what changed since version X?", then reads the current values from the table. It's synchronous with the transaction, has low overhead, and is great for syncing caches, mobile clients or search indexes, where only the latest state matters.
X: Change Data Capture is richer. It reads the transaction log asynchronously and records the full history of changes in change tables: inserts, deletes, and the before and after values of updates, with the order of operations. It's suited to auditing, data warehouse loading, and streaming changes to other systems. Tools like Debezium read CDC and publish each change as an event to Kafka, which is a common way to implement the outbox pattern or feed other services without changing application code.
X: The trade-offs: CDC uses more storage, needs SQL Server Agent jobs for capture and cleanup on-premise, and adds some latency and operational work. Change Tracking is simpler but loses intermediate values.
X: So: Change Tracking for "give me what's changed so I can sync", CDC for "give me every change, with history".

S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you seed reference data with EF Core?
K: ef core seed data, hasdata, seeding reference data, useseeding, migration data seeding, lookup tables seed
X: There are a few ways, and the right one depends on the kind of data.
X: HasData, in the model configuration, defines seed rows for an entity, with explicit primary key values. EF Core includes inserts, updates and deletes for that data in migrations, comparing with the previous model. It works well for small, stable reference data, like statuses, country codes or types, that should be identical in every environment. Its limitations: keys must be hard-coded, it can't depend on data already in the database, and changes to large seed sets create noisy migrations.

X: Custom migration code with migrationBuilder.Sql, or a post-deployment script in a database project, is another option, especially when the data change must happen at a precise point in the schema evolution.
X: For test data and local development, I keep it separate from reference data, in a seeding tool or test fixtures, never in production migrations.
X: In regulated systems, reference data changes are part of the validated release, reviewed like code. Configuration that differs per study or customer isn't seed data at all; it belongs in configuration tooling, like our Admin console.
@p17-255
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is row-level security in SQL Server?
K: row level security, rls sql server, security policy predicate, tenant isolation database, session_context
X: Row-level security lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who is running the query, without changing the queries.
X: I create an inline table-valued function, the predicate, that returns a row when access is allowed, like when the row's TenantId equals the tenant id stored in the session context. Then I create a security policy that applies the function as a filter predicate on the table, so SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE silently only see allowed rows, and optionally a block predicate, which prevents inserting or updating rows into another tenant.
X: For applications that connect with one shared database login, the user or tenant identity is set per connection with sp_set_session_context, for example through an EF Core connection interceptor right after the connection opens, and the predicate reads it with SESSION_CONTEXT.
X: It's a strong defence in depth for multi-tenant databases: even if a developer forgets a WHERE clause, or a reporting tool queries the table directly, data from other tenants isn't exposed.
X: The cautions. The predicate runs for every query, so it must be simple and backed by indexes, otherwise performance suffers. Session context must be reset correctly on pooled connections. Admin and maintenance processes need a way to bypass it safely. And it isn't a replacement for authorization in the application, which still decides what each user may do.
@p17-256
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is zone.js, and what does zoneless Angular mean?
K: zone.js, zoneless angular, ngzone, provideZonelessChangeDetection, run outside angular, change detection trigger
X: zone.js is a library that patches browser async APIs, like setTimeout, promises, DOM events and XHR, so Angular knows whenever some async work finishes. After any of these, Angular runs change detection to update the view. That's why, in classic Angular, changing a component property inside a click handler or an HTTP callback just works, without calling anything.
X: The downsides: it's a fairly heavy library, it triggers change detection very often, even when nothing relevant changed, async stack traces get harder to read, and native async/await can't be patched, so Angular had to downgrade it during builds.
X: The NgZone service lets you control it, for example runOutsideAngular for frequent events, like mousemove or a polling timer, so they don't trigger change detection on every tick.
X: Zoneless Angular removes zone.js entirely. Change detection is triggered explicitly by things Angular knows about: signals changing, the async pipe, event handlers bound in templates, and markForCheck. It was experimental in Angular 18, stable in 20, and it's the default for new apps since Angular 21, configured with provideZonelessChangeDetection in older versions.
X: The benefits are smaller bundles, better performance and cleaner debugging. Migrating requires components to work well with OnPush and signals, because code that changes state outside those triggers won't update the view anymore.
@p17-257
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is the new control flow syntax in Angular, like @if and @for?
K: angular control flow, @if @for @switch, built in control flow, ngif vs @if, track in @for
X: Since Angular 17, templates have built-in control flow blocks that replace the structural directives ngIf, ngFor and ngSwitch.
X: @if with an expression shows a block, with @else if and @else branches, and I can alias the result, like @if user of async as user. @switch with @case and @default replaces ngSwitch. @for loops over a collection, and it requires a track expression, like track item.id, which tells Angular how to identify each item, so it can reuse DOM elements instead of recreating them when the list changes. There's also an @empty block that shows when the collection is empty, and implicit variables like $index, $first, $last and $count.
X: The benefits: it's built into the compiler, so there's no need to import CommonModule or the directives; it's more readable, especially else branches, which used to need ng-template references; type narrowing works better inside @if blocks; and it's faster. The mandatory track also fixes a common performance mistake, because many teams forgot trackBy with ngFor, causing full re-rendering of lists.
X: The Angular CLI has a migration schematic, ng generate @angular/core:control-flow, that converts existing templates automatically.
X: In our newer Angular 17 study builder, we use the new syntax, while the older Angular 8 and 12 sub-apps still use the directives.
@p17-258
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are @defer blocks in Angular?
K: defer blocks, @defer angular, deferrable views, lazy load component template, on viewport, on idle
X: @defer, introduced in Angular 17, lazily loads part of a template and its dependencies. Components, directives and pipes used only inside the @defer block are split into a separate JavaScript chunk, which is downloaded and rendered only when a trigger condition happens.
X: The triggers include: on idle, the default, when the browser is idle; on viewport, when the placeholder scrolls into view; on interaction, when the user clicks or types in the placeholder; on hover; on timer, after a delay; on immediate; and when with a condition. There's also prefetch, so I can download the code earlier, like on idle, but render it later, on interaction.
X: Related blocks control what's shown meanwhile: @placeholder before loading starts, with an optional minimum display time to avoid flicker; @loading while the chunk downloads; and @error if loading fails.
X: It's useful for heavy parts of a page that aren't needed immediately: charts below the fold, a rich text editor, a comments section, or a big dialog. The initial bundle gets smaller, and the first render is faster, improving metrics like Largest Contentful Paint.
X: Before @defer, lazy loading in Angular was mainly at the route level, or manual dynamic imports with ViewContainerRef. Now it's declarative and fine-grained. With server-side rendering, Angular 19 added incremental hydration, where deferred blocks hydrate only when triggered.
@p17-259
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are signal inputs, model inputs and the output function in Angular?
K: signal inputs, input function angular, model signal, output function, input required, two way binding signals
X: Since Angular 17.1, components can declare inputs with the input function instead of the Input decorator: name equals input of string, or input.required of string. The input is a read-only signal, so in the template I read it as name(), and in code I can use it in computed signals, like fullName equals computed of first plus last. Angular updates the signal whenever the parent passes a new value. This replaces ngOnChanges and setters for reacting to input changes, and with required inputs, the compiler errors if the parent doesn't provide them. Transforms, like booleanAttribute, still work.
X: The model function creates a writable input for two-way binding. A child declares value equals model of number, and it can set it with value.set. The parent binds with the banana-in-a-box syntax, square brackets and parentheses, to a property or a signal, and changes flow both ways. It's much simpler than the old pattern of an Input plus an Output with the Change suffix.
X: The output function replaces the Output decorator with EventEmitter: saved equals output of Shipment, and I call saved.emit. It's lighter, and outputFromObservable can turn an RxJS stream into an output.
X: There are also signal-based queries: viewChild, viewChildren, contentChild and contentChildren, which return signals instead of being set later.
X: Together, they make components fully signal-based, which works well with OnPush and zoneless change detection.
@p17-260
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are computed and effect in Angular signals, and what are the pitfalls of effect?
K: computed signal, effect angular, signal effect pitfalls, untracked, derived state signals, allowsignalwrites
X: A computed signal derives its value from other signals: total equals computed of items() reduced to a sum. It's lazy and memoised: it only recalculates when one of the signals it read has changed, and only when someone reads it. It's read-only and should be a pure function. It's the right tool for derived state, like filtered lists, totals or flags.
X: An effect runs a side-effect function whenever the signals it reads change. It tracks dependencies automatically, runs at least once, and is cleaned up when its component is destroyed. Effects are meant for syncing with things outside Angular's signal world: writing to local storage, logging, calling a third-party chart library, or manual DOM work.
X: The pitfalls. Using effects to derive state, like an effect that sets another signal whenever a signal changes. That's what computed is for, and the effect version causes extra change detection cycles, timing issues, and possibly loops. Angular originally blocked signal writes inside effects by default for this reason. Unintended dependencies: every signal read inside the effect becomes a dependency, so reading something incidental re-runs the effect; untracked lets me read a signal without tracking it. Async work inside effects can race, so I use the cleanup function, onCleanup, to cancel previous work.
X: For data loading driven by signals, the newer resource and httpResource APIs are usually better than effects.
@p17-261
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are linkedSignal and the resource API in Angular?
K: linkedsignal, resource api angular, httpresource, rxresource, async data signals, loading state signals
X: These are newer signal APIs, introduced around Angular 19 and 20, that fill gaps between computed and writable signals, and between signals and async data.
X: linkedSignal creates a writable signal whose value is derived from other signals, but which the user can also set. When the source changes, it resets to a new computed value. The classic example is a selected option: the list of options comes from an input, and the selected item should default to the first option, but the user can change it. When the options list changes, the selection resets. Before, people did this with an effect that wrote to a signal, which was messy.
X: resource connects signals to asynchronous data. I give it a params function that reads signals, like the selected site id, and a loader function that fetches data. Whenever the parameters change, it calls the loader again, cancelling the previous request with an AbortSignal. It exposes signals for value, status, isLoading and error, so the template can show a spinner or an error easily. rxResource does the same with an Observable loader, and httpResource wraps HttpClient directly, so it works with interceptors.
X: These remove a lot of boilerplate for the common "reload data when a filter changes" pattern, and avoid race conditions from slower responses arriving after faster ones.
X: They're still evolving, so I check their stability status for the Angular version in use.
@p17-262
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do toSignal and toObservable work, and when do you use them?
K: tosignal, toobservable, rxjs signals interop, rxjs-interop, convert observable to signal
X: They're the bridge between RxJS and signals, from the rxjs-interop package.
X: toSignal subscribes to an Observable and gives back a signal with its latest value. I use it when a service exposes an Observable, like an HTTP call, route parameters or a store selector, but I want to use the value in a template or in computed signals. It subscribes immediately and unsubscribes automatically when the component or service is destroyed, so there's no manual subscription management. Since an Observable might not emit synchronously, the signal's initial value is undefined, unless I provide an initialValue, or use requireSync for observables that emit immediately, like a BehaviorSubject. Errors from the Observable are thrown when the signal is read, so I handle them in the stream first.
X: toObservable does the reverse: it turns a signal into an Observable that emits when the signal changes. That's useful when I need RxJS operators on signal values, like debounceTime and switchMap on a search term signal, to call an API and cancel outdated requests. Then I often convert the result back with toSignal.
X: Both must be called in an injection context, like a constructor or field initialiser, or be given an Injector.
X: My general approach: signals for synchronous state and templates, RxJS for complex async event streams, and these functions at the boundary.
@p17-263
S: ngx
D: A
T: inject() function vs constructor injection in Angular: what is the difference?
K: inject function angular, constructor injection angular, injection context, functional injection, inject vs constructor
X: Angular has two ways to get dependencies. Constructor injection declares them as constructor parameters, like constructor(private http: HttpClient). The inject function, available since Angular 14, gets them from inside the class body or a function: private http equals inject of HttpClient.
X: Both use the same injector hierarchy, so the dependency is the same. The differences are practical.
X: inject works in functions, not just classes. That enabled functional route guards, resolvers and HTTP interceptors, which are much shorter than class-based ones. It also allows reusable helper functions that inject things, like an injectStudyId function that reads the route.
X: Inheritance is easier: with constructor injection, a subclass must repeat all the base class's dependencies and pass them to super. With inject, the base class gets its own dependencies.
X: It works better with modern TypeScript and the useDefineForClassFields setting, where constructor parameter properties had ordering issues with field initialisers.
X: The constraint is that inject only works in an injection context: during construction, in field initialisers, in factory functions, or inside runInInjectionContext. Calling it later, like in ngOnInit or a click handler, throws an error.
X: The Angular team now recommends inject, and there's a migration schematic to convert constructor injection. For unit tests, both work the same way with TestBed.
@p17-264
S: ngx
D: A
T: How does Angular's hierarchical dependency injection work?
K: hierarchical injectors angular, providedin root, component providers, environment injector, element injector, service instance per component
X: Angular has a tree of injectors, and where a service is provided decides how many instances exist and who shares them.
X: At the top is the environment injector hierarchy. providedIn root in the Injectable decorator registers a singleton for the whole app, and it's tree-shakable: if nothing injects it, it's removed from the bundle. Services provided in an application's providers, or in a lazy-loaded route's providers, live in environment injectors. A lazy route with its own providers gets its own child injector, so a service provided there is a separate instance for that feature.
X: Then there's the element injector hierarchy, following the component tree. If a component lists a service in its providers array, each instance of that component gets its own instance of the service, shared with its children, and destroyed with the component. That's useful for state that belongs to one part of the screen, like a form wizard's state service or one editor instance per tab. viewProviders limits visibility to the component's own view, not projected content.
X: When a component injects something, Angular searches up the element injectors first, then the environment injectors, until it finds a provider. Modifiers change the search: Optional, Self, SkipSelf and Host, which are options on the inject function.
X: A common bug is accidentally providing a "global" service in a component's providers, creating separate instances and making shared state look broken.
@p17-265
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is an InjectionToken, and what are useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting?
K: injectiontoken, usefactory usevalue useclass useexisting, angular providers types, inject config angular, provide token
X: An InjectionToken is a key for dependency injection when there's no class to use as the key, like a configuration object, a primitive value, an interface, which doesn't exist at runtime in TypeScript, or a function. I create it with new InjectionToken of AppConfig with a description, and optionally a factory that provides a default value.
X: Providers then tell Angular what to give for a token or class.
X: useValue provides a fixed value, like an API base URL or a configuration object loaded at startup.
X: useClass provides an instance of a class, which lets me substitute an implementation: provide LoggerService, useClass ConsoleLoggerService. That's useful for environment-specific implementations or test doubles.
X: useFactory calls a function to create the value, and it can use inject inside, or a deps array in older code. It's for values that depend on other services or runtime conditions, like choosing a storage implementation based on configuration.
X: useExisting creates an alias: requesting one token returns the same instance as another. For example, a component can provide itself under an abstract token, so child components can inject it through an interface.
X: The multi flag lets several providers contribute to the same token, giving an array. Angular uses this for HTTP interceptors, form validators and app initialisers.
X: In our Angular apps, the API base URL and feature settings are provided through an InjectionToken filled from a runtime configuration file.
@p17-266
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are functional route guards and resolvers in Angular?
K: functional guards, canactivatefn, canmatch, resolver angular, resolvefn, route guard function
X: Since Angular 15, guards and resolvers can be plain functions instead of classes implementing interfaces like CanActivate. A guard has a type like CanActivateFn, receives the route and router state, and uses inject to get services. It returns true to allow, false to block, or a UrlTree to redirect, like to the login page, and it can return an Observable or Promise of these. Class-based guards are deprecated.
X: The guard types: canActivate, whether a route can be entered; canActivateChild, for child routes; canDeactivate, whether the user can leave, typically to warn about unsaved changes; and canMatch, whether a route definition should even be considered. canMatch is great for loading different components for the same path based on a role or feature flag, and it prevents the lazy-loaded code from downloading when the user isn't allowed.
X: Resolvers, ResolveFn, fetch data before the route activates, and the component receives it through the route data, or as an input when withComponentInputBinding is enabled.
X: I use resolvers sparingly. Navigation waits until the data arrives, so the user sees nothing happening on slow requests, and errors are harder to show nicely. Often it's better to navigate immediately and let the component show a loading state.
X: Guards are for user experience, not security: the API must still enforce authorization, because anyone can call it directly.
@p17-267
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you handle token refresh on 401 in an Angular interceptor?
K: token refresh interceptor, 401 retry angular, refresh token interceptor, queue requests during refresh, httpinterceptorfn auth
X: An auth interceptor adds the access token to outgoing requests, and handles expired tokens transparently.
X: The flow: the interceptor attaches the bearer token to requests going to our API, and only to our API's URLs, never to third-party domains. If a response comes back 401, it tries to refresh the token, and on success, retries the original request with the new token. If the refresh fails, it logs the user out and redirects to the login page.
X: The tricky part is concurrency. A screen often fires several requests at once, and they might all get 401 at the same time. Without care, each one triggers its own refresh, and with refresh token rotation, the second refresh uses an already-used refresh token and fails, logging the user out. So the interceptor keeps a single in-flight refresh: a flag plus a BehaviorSubject, or a shared Observable with shareReplay. The first 401 starts the refresh; other requests wait for it with filter and take of one, then retry with the new token.
X: Other details: don't intercept the refresh call itself, to avoid loops; retry each request only once; and refresh proactively before expiry when possible, which avoids most 401s. Libraries like angular-auth-oidc-client or keycloak-angular handle much of this.
X: In our apps, the Keycloak adapter refreshes tokens before expiry, and the interceptor attaches the current token.

T: How do you write custom sync and async validators in Angular reactive forms?
K: custom validator angular, async validator, validatorfn, asyncvalidatorfn, cross field validation angular, form group validator
X: A synchronous validator is a function that receives an AbstractControl and returns null if valid, or an errors object, like noFutureDate equals true, if invalid. X: An async validator returns an Observable or Promise of the errors or null. It's for checks that need the server, like "is this kit number valid and available?" or "is this username taken?". Angular runs async validators only after all sync validators pass, and the control's status is PENDING while it runs, which the UI can show as a small spinner.
X: To avoid calling the API on every keystroke, I use updateOn blur for that control, or debounce inside the validator using timer and switchMap, and make sure the Observable completes, with take of one or first, otherwise the form stays pending.
X: Server-side validation is still the source of truth, and I map server validation errors back to the form controls.

X: I usually define an interface for the form model, build the form with the form builder, and map the typed raw value to the API DTO. In Angular 21, there's also a new experimental signal-based forms API.

T: How do you build a dynamic form from configuration in Angular?

X: Dynamic forms are generated at runtime from a configuration or metadata, instead of being hard-coded in a template. That's essential when forms vary by customer or by study, like screening questions in a clinical trial, where each study defines its own questions, types and rules.

X: The server must apply the same rules, ideally from the same configuration, because client-side validation can be bypassed.
X: Our IRT has dynamic forms with rule expressions for screening, configured per study in the study builder.

T: What is ControlValueAccessor, and when do you implement it?
K: controlvalueaccessor, custom form control angular, ng_value_accessor, formcontrolname custom component, writevalue registeronchange
X: ControlValueAccessor is the interface that connects an Angular form control to a UI element. Built-in accessors exist for inputs, selects and checkboxes. When I build my own input component, like a date range picker, a kit quantity stepper or a searchable site selector, and I want it to work with formControlName and ngModel just like a native input, I implement ControlValueAccessor.
X: It has four methods. writeValue is called by the forms API to set the component's value, for example when the form is initialised or patched. registerOnChange gives me a callback that I call whenever the user changes the value, so the form control updates. registerOnTouched gives me a callback to call when the user leaves the control, usually on blur, which drives the touched state for showing validation messages. setDisabledState, which is optional, is called when the control is enabled or disabled.

X: The benefit is that complex widgets become first-class form controls: validation, disabled state, reset and value changes all work consistently, and forms using them stay clean.

S: ngx

T: How do you create a custom structural directive?
K: custom structural directive, templateref viewcontainerref, star syntax directive, permission directive angular, createembeddedview
X: A structural directive changes the DOM structure by adding or removing elements, like the built-in ngIf did. I write one when I have reusable display logic, like showing content only if the user has a certain permission.
X: For example, a hasPermission directive, used as an asterisk hasPermission equals 'kits.return' on an element. The asterisk is shorthand: Angular wraps the element in an ng-template and passes it to the directive.
X: Inside the directive, I inject TemplateRef, which represents that template, and ViewContainerRef, which is the place in the DOM where views can be inserted. When the input value, the permission name, is set, or the user's permissions change, the directive checks the permission. I can support an else template too, through a second input.
X: I can also pass a context object to the template, which lets the directive expose variables to the template using let syntax, the way the old ngFor exposed index.
X: With signals, the input can be a signal input, and an effect or computed drives the view creation.
X: Again, this is only for user experience: hiding a button doesn't secure anything; the API enforces the permission.
@p17-273
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you write a custom pipe, and when should it be impure?
K: custom pipe angular, pipe transform, pure vs impure pipe example, standalone pipe, format pipe
X: A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, like formatting a date or a status label. To create one, I write a class with the Pipe decorator, giving it a name, and implement PipeTransform with a transform method that takes the value and optional arguments and returns the display value. In modern Angular, pipes are standalone by default, and components import them directly.
X: For example, a kitStatus pipe that converts a status code into a friendly label, or a siteTime pipe that formats a UTC timestamp in the site's time zone. Usage is kit.status piped into kitStatus, or created piped into siteTime with the time zone as an argument.
X: Pipes are pure by default. A pure pipe is only re-executed when its input value changes by reference, or its arguments change. That makes them very efficient, and much better than calling a method in the template, which runs on every change detection cycle. So pure pipes should be pure functions: no side effects, same output for the same input.
X: An impure pipe, with pure set to false, runs on every change detection cycle. It's needed when the output depends on something other than the input reference, like a mutable array that changes internally, or external state. The async pipe is the famous impure pipe. Impure pipes must be very cheap, otherwise they slow the whole page.
X: Often a better alternative to an impure pipe is immutable data, or a computed signal.
@p17-274
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is the async pipe, and why is it recommended?
K: async pipe, async pipe benefits, subscribe in template, observable in template, async pipe change detection
X: The async pipe subscribes to an Observable or Promise in the template and returns the latest emitted value. For example, shipments$ piped into async.
X: It's recommended for several reasons. Automatic subscription management: it subscribes when the component is rendered and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so there are no memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions. It works well with OnPush change detection, because it marks the component for check whenever a new value arrives, so the view updates even though no input changed. And it leads to a declarative style: the component exposes streams, and the template consumes them, without manual subscribe calls that copy values into component fields.
X: A few things to watch. Each async pipe on the same Observable creates a separate subscription, so for an HTTP Observable used in several places, I'd cause several HTTP calls. The fix is to subscribe once with @if, using the as syntax to alias the value, or to share the stream with shareReplay. Errors in the stream need handling with catchError in the component, otherwise the subscription ends.
X: With signals, toSignal plays a similar role: it converts the Observable to a signal once, and the template reads it without a pipe. In newer code, I often use that, but the async pipe remains a perfectly good pattern, especially in existing RxJS-heavy apps like our older Angular sub-apps.

T: What are ng-template, ng-container and ngTemplateOutlet?
K: ng-template, ng-container, ngtemplateoutlet, template reference angular, reusable template, no extra dom element
X: ng-template defines a block of template that isn't rendered by itself. It's a template that something else can render later, possibly several times, with different data. Structural directives use it behind the scenes, and in older code, else branches pointed to an ng-template.
X: ng-container is a grouping element that doesn't produce any DOM element. It's useful when I need to apply logic to several elements without adding a wrapper div that would break the layout or CSS, like inside a table row or a flex container. It was commonly used to combine ngIf and ngFor, since only one structural directive is allowed per element.

It's the key to customisable components. For example, a reusable data table component can accept an ng-template for how to display a cell, through a content child query or an input. The table renders that template for each row with ngTemplateOutlet, passing the row as context. The consumer controls the cell markup, and the table controls the layout, sorting and paging.
X: The same idea lets me define a piece of markup once in a template, like a status badge layout, and render it in several places without creating a separate component.
@p17-276
S: ngx
D: A
T: How does view encapsulation and component styling work in Angular?
K: view encapsulation, emulated encapsulation, shadow dom angular, :host selector, ng-deep, component styles
X: Angular scopes component styles so a component's CSS doesn't leak out and affect other components. The ViewEncapsulation setting controls how.
X: Emulated is the default. Angular adds unique attributes to the component's elements and rewrites its CSS selectors to include those attributes, so styles only apply inside that component's template. ShadowDom uses the browser's real Shadow DOM, giving true isolation, but global styles, like a design system's base styles, don't reach inside. None makes the component's styles global, which is occasionally used for theme files, but it risks conflicts.
X: Special selectors: :host styles the component's own host element, like making it display block, and :host with a class lets the component react to a class on itself. :host-context applies styles based on an ancestor, like a dark theme class higher up.
X: To style inside a child component, especially third-party ones like Angular Material, people use ::ng-deep, which disables encapsulation for that rule. It's deprecated, though still widely used, because there's no full replacement. Better options are the child component's inputs, CSS custom properties, which pass through encapsulation, or the library's theming APIs.
X: In a large app, I keep component styles small, use a shared design system for consistency, and rely on CSS variables for theming. We keep the Angular sub-apps visually consistent with the React shell through shared design tokens.
@p17-277
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is server-side rendering and hydration in Angular?
K: angular ssr, hydration angular, angular universal, prerendering, incremental hydration, ssr benefits
X: Server-side rendering means the Angular app runs on the server, in Node.js, and returns fully rendered HTML for the requested page. The browser can show the content immediately, before the JavaScript has downloaded and started. That improves first paint and Largest Contentful Paint, helps SEO, and gives good link previews for social media, since crawlers see real content.
X: It used to be called Angular Universal. Since Angular 17, SSR is built into the CLI: ng new with the ssr option, or ng add @angular/ssr. Prerendering, or static site generation, renders pages at build time for content that doesn't change per request.
X: Hydration is what happens next in the browser. Instead of throwing away the server HTML and re-rendering everything, which caused flicker, Angular reuses the existing DOM and attaches event listeners and state to it. Full hydration has been stable since Angular 16. Event replay captures clicks that happen before hydration finishes and replays them. Incremental hydration, in Angular 19 and later, hydrates @defer blocks only when triggered, reducing JavaScript work further.
X: The challenges: code must not touch browser-only objects, like window or localStorage, during server rendering, so I guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender, and HTTP data fetched on the server is transferred to avoid fetching it twice.
X: For internal, login-only business apps like ours, SSR adds little, so we don't use it; it matters most for public, content-heavy sites.

T: How do you load runtime configuration in an Angular app instead of build-time environments?
K: runtime config angular, app initializer, provideappinitializer, environment.ts vs runtime config, config.json angular, build once deploy many
X: Angular's environment files are compiled into the bundle at build time. That means a separate build for each environment, which goes against "build once, deploy many", where the same tested artifact is promoted from test to UAT to production. In a validated environment, that matters, because a rebuilt artifact isn't the artifact that was tested.
X: So I load configuration at runtime. The app ships with a config.json file, or the server provides it at a known URL, containing environment-specific values like the API base URL, the identity provider URL, the client id and feature flags. The deployment pipeline writes the correct file for each environment, or the server generates it.

A config service stores the values, and other services read from it, or I provide individual values through InjectionTokens. Another approach is fetching the config in main.ts before calling bootstrapApplication, and passing it into the providers.
X: Only non-secret values go in this file, since the browser can read everything.
X: For our React shell, we use Vite environment variables, but the same principle applies, [and the older Angular sub-apps read their settings from the hosting MVC page].

T: How do you upgrade an Angular application across many versions, like 8 to 17?
K: angular upgrade, upgrade angular 8 to 17, ng update, angular migration versions, update angular major version
X: Angular officially supports upgrading one major version at a time, so going from 8 to 17 is nine steps, not one jump. I'd plan it as a project.
X: First, preparation. Make sure there's a good test suite and an end-to-end smoke test, because each step needs verifying. Check the third-party libraries, since they're usually the real blocker: each library needs a version compatible with each Angular version, and some are abandoned, so they must be replaced. Also check the Node.js and TypeScript versions each Angular version needs.
X: Then, step by step, using the Angular Update Guide at angular.dev/update, which lists the changes for each version pair. Keeping each step in its own commit or branch makes problems easy to isolate.
X: The big milestones along the way: Ivy becoming the only engine in version 12 and 13, which removed View Engine and broke old libraries; the removal of IE11 support; strict typed forms in 14; standalone components in 14 and 15; and the builder change to esbuild and the new control flow in 17. Those later features are optional migrations, which I'd do after the upgrade itself.
X: Our older sub-apps are on Angular 8 and 12, and the plan has been to move modules to React rather than upgrade them all.
