D: A
T: How do you add tests to legacy code that has none?
K: testing legacy code, characterization tests, seams, working effectively with legacy code, refactor without tests
X: Legacy code without tests is risky to change, but you can't stop and write tests for everything. I follow the approach from Working Effectively with Legacy Code: add tests where you're about to change things.
X: Characterisation tests first. Before changing a piece of code, I write tests that capture what it currently does, not what it should do. Call it with representative inputs and assert whatever it currently returns. Snapshot tools like Verify make this quick for complex outputs. These tests protect existing behaviour, including odd behaviour that other parts of the system may rely on.
X: Find or create seams. Legacy code often creates its dependencies directly: new SqlConnection, static calls, DateTime.Now, HttpContext.Current. A seam is a place where behaviour can be replaced for testing without editing the logic. Techniques: extract an interface and inject it; extract the hard-to-test call into a virtual method and override it in a test subclass; wrap static calls behind a small adapter; or pass values in as parameters. I make these changes in small, safe, often tool-assisted refactoring steps.
X: Sprout and wrap. For new functionality, I write it as a new, tested class or method, and call it from the legacy code, rather than adding more untested lines into a huge method.
X: Integration tests around the edges, like running the real API or stored procedure against a test database, often give the most protection quickly for very tangled code.
X: In our .NET Framework core, this is how we change risky areas safely.

D: A
T: How would you test a randomisation algorithm in a clinical trial system?
K: test randomization algorithm, randomisation testing, statistical testing allocation, test treatment allocation, irt randomization validation
X: Randomisation decides which treatment arm a patient gets, so mistakes affect the scientific validity of a trial. Testing it needs both normal tests and statistical checks.
X: Deterministic unit tests. The algorithm should take its random source as a dependency, so tests can supply a seeded generator or a predefined sequence. Then I assert exact outcomes for specific scenarios: with block size four and a 1:1 ratio, each block contains two of each arm; stratification puts patients into the right stratum based on their factors; when a site or stratum is capped, the right behaviour follows; and with a pre-generated randomisation list, patients receive the next entry in their stratum in order, and no list entry is used twice.
X: Edge cases: the last slot in a block, a list running out, invalid strata, concurrent randomisations at two sites at the same moment, which must not take the same entry, and re-randomisation rules.
X: Statistical simulation. Run the algorithm many thousands of times, [like 100,000 simulated patients], and check that the allocation ratios match the design within expected tolerance, that balance holds within strata and sites for dynamic methods like minimisation, and that there's no predictable pattern. These simulations run as part of study configuration testing, not every build.
X: Validation evidence. In a regulated system, the tests, the simulation reports and the configuration they ran against are kept as validation evidence, and the study's configuration is tested in UAT before it goes live.

S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test both states of a feature flag?
K: test feature flags, feature toggle testing, flag combinations testing, feature flag test strategy
X: Feature flags double the paths through the code, so the risk is that one state, usually the one not active in the test environment, is never tested and breaks when someone flips the flag.
X: My approach.
X: Unit tests for both states of each flag that changes logic. The flag check is injected, through IFeatureManager or a small interface, so tests set it on or off directly. Each flagged behaviour gets a test with the flag on and with it off.
X: Integration and end-to-end tests run against the configuration production will actually use at release. If production will have the flag off at first, the main test run uses off, plus a second run, or a subset of tests, with it on. Test environments shouldn't just have every flag on, because then the off path, which is what production is running, isn't tested.
X: Avoid testing every combination. With several flags, combinations explode. Flags should be independent where possible, and I test combinations only for flags that interact.
X: Test the flip itself for important flags: switching a flag at runtime shouldn't break in-flight requests or leave inconsistent state, like jobs started under the old behaviour.
X: Test the failure default: if the flag service is unreachable, the code should fall back to the safe value.
X: And when a flag is removed after full rollout, the tests for the dead path are removed too, which keeps the test suite honest about what the code actually does.

T: How do you test Azure Functions or AWS Lambda handlers?

D: A
T: How do you set up OpenTelemetry in a .NET service?
K: opentelemetry dotnet setup, otel dotnet, addopentelemetry, otlp exporter, instrument aspnet core opentelemetry
X: OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. In .NET, the runtime already produces the raw signals: Activity for traces, System.Diagnostics.Metrics for metrics, and ILogger for logs. OpenTelemetry collects and exports them.
X: Setup in Program.cs: builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry(), then ConfigureResource to set the service name, version and environment, which every signal carries. WithTracing adds instrumentation for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SQL client or EF Core, plus any custom ActivitySource the app defines. WithMetrics adds ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and runtime instrumentation, which gives request durations, GC, thread pool and exception counts, plus custom Meters. Logging gets builder.Logging.AddOpenTelemetry so logs carry the trace and span ids. Then UseOtlpExporter sends everything over OTLP, usually to a local OpenTelemetry Collector, which forwards to the backend, like Datadog, Grafana, Azure Monitor or CloudWatch. The endpoint and headers come from standard environment variables, like OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, so the same code works everywhere.
X: Good habits: name custom spans and metrics with clear, stable names; add useful attributes, like tenant or study id, but never personal data; record exceptions on spans; and filter out noise, like health check requests.
X: Our newest services use OpenTelemetry with Datadog, while older parts log to Splunk with Serilog. Standardising on OpenTelemetry means changing the backend later is configuration, not code.
@p17-586
S: obx
D: A
T: What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do, and why use one?
K: opentelemetry collector, otel collector, collector pipeline receivers processors exporters, agent vs gateway collector
X: The OpenTelemetry Collector is a separate process that receives telemetry, processes it, and exports it to one or more backends. Applications send to the collector over OTLP instead of talking to vendors directly.
X: Its configuration has pipelines for traces, metrics and logs, each built from receivers, processors and exporters. Receivers accept data: OTLP from apps, Prometheus scraping, host metrics, log files, Kafka and more. Processors transform it: batching for efficiency, memory limiting, adding resource attributes like cluster and region, filtering out noisy spans like health checks, redacting sensitive attributes, and tail-based sampling. Exporters send it on: to Datadog, Grafana, Jaeger, Prometheus, Azure Monitor, CloudWatch or several at once.
X: Why it's worth having. Applications stay simple and vendor-neutral; switching or adding a backend is a collector config change, not a redeploy of every service. Exports are offloaded: retries and buffering happen in the collector, so a backend outage doesn't slow the app. Central control: redaction, sampling and enrichment rules are applied consistently for all services. And credentials for the backend live in one place, not in every app.
X: Deployment patterns: an agent collector per host or as a sidecar or DaemonSet, close to apps, plus optionally a gateway collector cluster for central processing like tail sampling.
X: The collector itself must be monitored, since it's now part of the pipeline, and sized properly so it doesn't drop data under load.
@p17-587
S: obx
D: A
T: Counter vs gauge vs histogram: which metric type do you use when?
K: metric types, counter gauge histogram, updowncounter, percentile metrics, system diagnostics metrics
X: Choosing the right metric type decides what questions you can answer later.
X: A counter only goes up: requests handled, orders created, errors, bytes sent. You never look at its raw value; you look at its rate, like requests per second, or increase over a window. Counters survive restarts in Prometheus-style systems because rate functions handle resets.
X: An up-down counter or gauge represents a current value that goes up and down. An up-down counter is for things you increment and decrement, like active connections or items in an in-memory queue. A gauge is observed at a point in time, like memory used, queue depth read from the broker, or temperature of a storage unit. For gauges, averages and maximums over time make sense; rates don't.
X: A histogram records the distribution of values, like request duration or payload size, into buckets. From it you can compute percentiles, like p95 and p99 latency, which matter much more than averages, because averages hide the slow requests real users notice. Histograms can also be aggregated across instances correctly, which pre-computed percentiles can't.
X: In .NET's System.Diagnostics.Metrics, these are Counter, UpDownCounter, ObservableGauge and Histogram. For example, an allocation service might have a counter for allocations by outcome, a histogram for allocation duration, and an observable gauge for available kits per depot.
X: Bucket boundaries for histograms should cover the expected range, or exponential histograms can be used to avoid choosing them by hand.

D: A
T: How do you add custom business metrics to a .NET service?
K: custom metrics dotnet, meter dotnet, business metrics, system.diagnostics.metrics, imeterfactory, instrument business events
X: Technical metrics, like CPU and request latency, tell you whether the system is running. Business metrics tell you whether it's doing its job: orders placed, patients randomised, shipments delivered, allocations failed due to no stock. Often a business metric drops before any technical alarm fires, like an integration silently sending nothing.
X: In .NET, I use System.Diagnostics.Metrics. Get a Meter from IMeterFactory through dependency injection, which makes it testable, and create instruments once: a Counter for randomisations, a Histogram for end-to-end shipment processing time, an ObservableGauge for kits available per depot computed from a cached query. Record values where the business event happens, with tags for dimensions, like outcome success or failure, or region.
X: OpenTelemetry metrics, with AddMeter for the meter name, export them to the backend alongside the built-in metrics.
X: Design rules. Tags must have low cardinality: outcome, region, study phase, maybe study id if the number of studies is bounded, but never patient ids, kit numbers, or user ids, which would create millions of time series and huge costs. Name metrics consistently, with units, following OpenTelemetry naming conventions. Record at the point of truth, after the transaction commits, so failed transactions aren't counted as successes.
X: Then dashboards show business flow at a glance, and alerts can fire on "no randomisations in the last hour during business hours at an active study", which is exactly the kind of silent failure our AlertWatchDog jobs were built to catch.
@p17-589
S: obx
D: A
T: What are SLIs, SLOs and error budgets?
K: sli slo sla, error budget, service level objective, service level indicator, reliability targets
X: These come from site reliability engineering and give a precise way to talk about reliability.
X: An SLI, service level indicator, is a measurement of user experience, usually a ratio of good events to total events. For example: the percentage of API requests that succeed, the percentage served within 300 milliseconds, or the percentage of shipment events processed within five minutes.
X: An SLO, service level objective, is the target for an SLI over a window: 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 28 days, or 95 percent of requests complete within 300 milliseconds.
X: An SLA is a contract with customers, with consequences, like credits, if it's missed. SLOs should be stricter than SLAs, so you get warning before breaching a contract.
X: The error budget is what the SLO allows to fail: with 99.9 percent, that's 0.1 percent, roughly 43 minutes of full downtime in 30 days. It turns reliability into a shared, measurable resource. If the budget is healthy, the team can ship faster and take more risk. If it's being burned quickly, the team slows down releases and prioritises reliability work.
X: Alerting on SLOs uses burn rates: alert when the budget is being consumed much faster than sustainable, like 14 times the normal rate over an hour, which catches real user-facing problems while ignoring blips.
X: Choosing SLOs: base them on what users actually need, not 100 percent, which is impossible and makes every change risky.
@p17-590
S: obx
D: A
T: What are the RED and USE methods for monitoring?
K: red method, use method, rate errors duration, utilization saturation errors, golden signals, what to monitor
X: They're two simple checklists for what to monitor, from different angles.
X: The RED method is for services, from the user's point of view. For every service or endpoint, track Rate, the number of requests per second; Errors, the number or percentage of failed requests; and Duration, the distribution of response times, as percentiles. If you have these three for every service, you can quickly see which service is unhappy and how. They map well to dashboards: one row per service with three panels.
X: The USE method is for resources, from the infrastructure's point of view. For every resource, like CPU, memory, disk, network, connection pools, thread pools and queues, track Utilisation, how busy it is as a percentage of time or capacity; Saturation, how much extra work is waiting, like the run queue, queue length or thread pool queue; and Errors, like disk errors or dropped packets. Saturation is the one people forget, and it's often the most telling: 70 percent CPU might be fine, but a growing thread pool queue is a real problem.
X: Google's four golden signals are similar: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
X: How I use them together: RED tells me there's a problem, like the allocation API's p95 latency has tripled. USE on the resources behind it tells me why, like the database connection pool is saturated with requests waiting for connections.
@p17-591
S: obx
D: A
T: What is high cardinality, and why does it blow up metrics cost?
K: high cardinality metrics, metric labels cardinality, time series explosion, metrics cost, label best practices
X: Every unique combination of a metric name and its label values is a separate time series. A request counter with labels for method, route and status code might produce a few hundred series, which is fine. Add a label for user id, and it becomes hundreds of thousands. That's high cardinality.
X: Why it's a problem. Metrics backends store and index each series separately, so memory, storage and query time grow with the number of series. Prometheus can run out of memory; commercial tools, like Datadog, bill per custom metric series, so a single careless label can create a huge bill overnight. Queries and dashboards slow down too.
X: Common culprits: user ids, email addresses, request ids, raw URLs with ids in the path instead of route templates, timestamps, exception messages, kit or order numbers, and pod names in very dynamic environments.
X: How I avoid it. Use bounded values for labels: route templates like /shipments/{id}, status code classes, region, outcome. Put high-cardinality detail in traces and logs instead, which are designed for per-request data and searchable by id. Set up review of new metrics and limits in the pipeline or collector, which can drop or rewrite labels. Monitor the number of series per metric to catch growth.
X: If you need per-entity analysis, like latency per customer, that's often better answered by querying logs or traces, or with an analytics store designed for high cardinality.
@p17-592
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you choose log levels, and what belongs at each level?
K: log levels, when to log error vs warning, log level guidelines, information vs debug logging, too many logs
X: Consistent log levels make logs useful and keep costs down. My guidelines:
X: Critical or Fatal: the application or a key component can't continue, like failing to start because configuration is invalid, or losing the database entirely. Someone should be woken up.
X: Error: an operation failed and needs attention, like an unhandled exception in a request, a message moved to the dead-letter queue, or an integration call that failed after all retries. Each error log should be actionable; if nobody should do anything about it, it isn't an error.
X: Warning: something unexpected happened, but the system handled it, like a retry succeeded after a transient failure, a fallback was used, a slow query crossed a threshold, or a deprecated API was called. Warnings help spot trends before they become errors.
X: Information: significant business and lifecycle events: service started, shipment created, randomisation completed, a job processed 230 records. They tell the story of what the system did, without detail of every step.
X: Debug and Trace: detailed diagnostic data for developers, like intermediate values and branching decisions. Off in production by default, but switchable per category at runtime, so we can turn it on for one component during an investigation.
X: Other rules: log an exception once, at the place where it's handled, not at every layer; use structured properties, not string concatenation; never log secrets or personal data; and set per-namespace minimum levels to silence noisy libraries.
@p17-593
S: obx
D: A
T: Head-based vs tail-based sampling: how do you sample traces?
K: trace sampling, head based sampling, tail based sampling, sampling rate opentelemetry, keep error traces
X: At high traffic, recording every trace is expensive in network, storage and money, and most successful traces look the same. Sampling keeps a representative subset.
X: Head-based sampling decides at the start of a trace, in the first service, usually as a percentage, like keep 10 percent. The decision is propagated in the trace context, so all downstream services keep or drop the same trace, and traces stay complete. It's simple, cheap and done in the SDK, with ParentBased and TraceIdRatioBased samplers in OpenTelemetry. The downside: the decision is made before you know whether the request will fail or be slow, so you drop 90 percent of your interesting error traces too.
X: Tail-based sampling decides after the trace has completed, typically in an OpenTelemetry Collector or the backend, which buffers all spans of a trace for a short time. Then rules decide: keep every trace with an error, keep every trace slower than one second, keep traces for specific important endpoints, and keep a small percentage of the rest. You get all the interesting traces and few boring ones. The cost: the collector must receive all spans and hold them in memory, and all spans of a trace must reach the same collector instance, which needs load balancing by trace id.
X: A common combination: no or light head sampling at the SDK, tail sampling in a collector gateway.
X: Metrics should be computed before sampling, so rates and error percentages stay accurate.
@p17-594
S: obx
D: A
T: How does trace context propagate across HTTP calls and message queues?
K: trace context propagation, traceparent header, w3c trace context, propagate trace through rabbitmq, distributed tracing messages
X: Distributed tracing only works if every hop passes the trace context along, so each service's spans join the same trace.
X: The standard is W3C Trace Context. The traceparent header carries the trace id, the parent span id and sampling flags, and tracestate carries vendor-specific data. Baggage, a separate header, carries application key-value pairs, like tenant id, that should travel with the request, used carefully because it's sent everywhere.
X: For HTTP, .NET does it automatically: HttpClient instrumentation adds traceparent to outgoing requests, and ASP.NET Core reads it on incoming requests, creating a child Activity. Most other languages' OpenTelemetry instrumentations do the same, which is what makes mixed .NET and Java systems traceable end to end.
X: For messaging, it's more manual and more often broken. The producer must inject the trace context into message headers or application properties, and the consumer must extract it and start its processing span with a link or as a child. Some client libraries have instrumentation that does this, like for Kafka, Azure Service Bus, MassTransit and NServiceBus; for raw RabbitMQ clients, I add small helpers using OpenTelemetry's propagator API to inject and extract. For batch consumers, span links connect one processing span to the many producer spans.
X: Where context is lost, like a legacy system in the middle or a file transfer, I carry a correlation id in the payload and log it, so the pieces can still be joined.
@p17-595
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you design a useful Grafana dashboard?
K: grafana dashboard design, dashboard best practices, service dashboard, too many panels, dashboard hierarchy
X: A good dashboard answers specific questions quickly, especially at 3 AM during an incident. Most bad dashboards have too many panels and no story.
X: How I design them.
X: Start from questions. Is the service healthy for users? What changed? Which dependency is the problem? Each panel should help answer one of them.
X: Use a hierarchy. A top-level overview shows every service's health in one place, with RED metrics: request rate, error percentage and latency percentiles, plus SLO status. Clicking through goes to a service dashboard with detail: endpoints, dependencies, resource usage with USE metrics, queue depths. Then deeper, component dashboards, like database or message broker.
X: Top of the page is the most important: the user-facing signals and SLOs. Below, the causes: dependencies, saturation, infrastructure.
X: Make it comparable: show deployments and incidents as annotations, so "latency went up right after release 3.4.2" is obvious. Use consistent time ranges and units, percentiles instead of averages, and the same colours for the same meaning.
X: Use template variables for environment, region and service, so one dashboard serves all of them, instead of copies that drift.
X: Link out: from a latency spike to the traces for that time range, through exemplars, and to the logs.
X: Keep dashboards as code, in JSON or with Terraform or Grafana's provisioning, reviewed in pull requests, so they don't rot.
X: Finally, delete dashboards nobody uses; a few trusted dashboards beat a hundred abandoned ones.
@p17-596
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you reduce alert fatigue?
K: alert fatigue, too many alerts, noisy alerts, actionable alerts, on call burnout, alert tuning
X: Alert fatigue happens when people receive so many alerts, mostly unimportant or false, that they start ignoring them, and then miss the real one. It's a reliability risk and a morale problem.
X: How I reduce it.
X: Every page must be actionable and urgent. If the response is "wait and see" or "nothing to do", it shouldn't wake anyone. Those become tickets, dashboard items or daily digests.
X: Alert on symptoms, not causes. Users care about errors, latency and failed business processes, so alerts are based on SLOs and burn rates. High CPU on one instance is a cause; if users aren't affected, it's not a page.
X: Tune thresholds and durations. A one-minute spike shouldn't page; require the condition for a sensible period, use hysteresis so alerts don't flap, and use dynamic thresholds where traffic varies a lot by time of day.
X: Deduplicate and group: one incident should produce one notification, not fifty from every instance and every dependent service. Dependencies, like "database down", can suppress downstream alerts.
X: Route correctly: alerts go to the owning team, with severity levels deciding paging versus messaging.
X: Include context: a clear title, the affected service and impact, a link to the dashboard and a runbook.
X: Review regularly: after each on-call week, look at which alerts fired, which were useful, and fix or delete the noisy ones. Tracking alerts per week as a metric keeps the pressure on.
@p17-597
S: obx
D: A
T: What is synthetic monitoring, and when do you need it?
K: synthetic monitoring, synthetic checks, uptime checks, canary scripts, cloudwatch synthetics, availability tests
X: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted checks against the system on a schedule, from outside, as if it were a user: every few minutes, call the health endpoint, log in, open the dashboard, search for a shipment, and confirm the results look right.
X: Why it's needed alongside real-user monitoring and server metrics. It detects problems when there's no traffic: at night or weekends, or for a feature rarely used, real users won't reveal an outage until Monday morning; synthetics will. It tests from the user's side, so it catches failures that server metrics can't see: DNS problems, expired certificates, CDN or load balancer misconfiguration, a broken login flow with the identity provider, or a front-end bundle error. It provides a consistent baseline for availability and latency from different regions, useful for SLA reporting. And it can run right after a deployment as an automated smoke test.
X: Types: simple uptime checks on URLs, with status code, content and certificate expiry checks; API checks with multi-step calls; and browser checks, scripted with Playwright or Selenium, that run full user journeys.
X: Tools: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, Azure Application Insights availability tests, Datadog Synthetics, Grafana synthetic monitoring, or a simple scheduled Playwright job.
X: Care points: use dedicated test accounts and test data, so synthetic transactions never pollute production data or reports, which in a clinical system is critical; never create real patient or shipment records; and keep scripts maintained, or they become noisy false alarms.
@p17-598
S: obx
D: A
T: What is real user monitoring, and which front-end metrics matter?
K: real user monitoring, rum, core web vitals, lcp inp cls, front end monitoring, page performance real users
X: Real user monitoring collects performance and error data from actual users' browsers. A small script or SDK in the app reports page loads, route changes, API call timings, JavaScript errors and user sessions. Unlike synthetic tests from a fast data centre, it shows what people on real devices, networks and locations experience.
X: The key metrics are Google's Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint, LCP: how quickly the main content appears, with a good target under 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint, INP, which replaced First Input Delay: how quickly the page responds to clicks and key presses, good under 200 milliseconds. Cumulative Layout Shift, CLS: how much content jumps around while loading, good under 0.1. Also useful: Time to First Byte, for server and network speed, and for single-page apps, the duration of route changes and key API calls.
X: Look at percentiles, like the 75th, which Core Web Vitals use, and segment by page, browser, country and device, because averages hide the users having a bad time.
X: RUM tools also capture JavaScript errors with stack traces mapped through source maps, and can link front-end sessions to back-end traces using trace context headers, so a slow screen can be followed into the API and database.
X: Tools: Datadog RUM, Azure Application Insights for JavaScript, CloudWatch RUM, Sentry, or the open-source web-vitals library reporting to your own backend.
X: Privacy matters: mask inputs and never capture personal or clinical data in session replays.
@p17-599
S: obx
D: A
T: What are exemplars, and how do they connect metrics to traces?
K: exemplars, metrics to traces, exemplar prometheus, link metric spike to trace, grafana exemplars
X: Metrics are aggregated, which makes them cheap and great for spotting problems, but they lose the detail: the latency histogram shows p99 jumped to three seconds, but not which requests were slow or why. Traces have the detail, but finding the right trace among millions is hard. Exemplars bridge that gap.
X: An exemplar is a sample data point attached to a metric value, carrying the trace id of a specific request that contributed to it. When the service records a request duration in a histogram, the OpenTelemetry SDK can attach the current trace id as an exemplar for that bucket. Backends like Prometheus, Grafana Mimir and others store a few exemplars alongside the metric.
X: In Grafana, exemplars appear as dots on the latency graph. During an incident, I see the spike, hover over a dot in the slow area, and click straight into the trace in Tempo or another tracing backend. That trace shows exactly where time was spent: maybe a database call that took 2.8 seconds. From the trace, I jump to logs filtered by the same trace id.
X: So the investigation flow becomes metric to trace to logs, in a few clicks, instead of guessing time ranges and searching.
X: To make it work: the SDK must have exemplars enabled, which OpenTelemetry .NET supports with an exemplar filter, the trace must be sampled, otherwise the link leads nowhere, and the backend must support storing exemplars.
X: Commercial APM tools offer similar navigation built in.
@p17-600
S: obx
D: A
T: What is Prometheus, and how do you write basic PromQL queries?
K: prometheus, promql, prometheus scraping, rate function promql, histogram_quantile, prometheus basics
X: Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system and time-series database. It pulls metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints, usually /metrics, on each target at an interval, like every 15 seconds. In Kubernetes, it discovers targets automatically through service discovery and annotations or ServiceMonitor resources. .NET apps expose metrics through the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter, or push via OTLP to Prometheus versions that accept it.
X: Data is time series identified by a metric name and labels, like http_server_request_duration_seconds with method, route and status code.
X: Basic PromQL patterns I use often.
X: Request rate: sum by (route) of rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]). rate computes per-second increase of a counter over the window.
X: Error percentage: the rate of requests with status code 5xx divided by the rate of all requests, times 100.
X: Latency percentile: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))). The le label holds histogram bucket boundaries.
X: Saturation, like memory used versus limit per pod, with division between two metrics matched on labels.
X: Alerting rules use the same expressions with a for duration, evaluated by Prometheus and routed through Alertmanager, which groups, silences and routes notifications.
X: For long-term storage and multiple clusters, Prometheus is often combined with Thanos, Mimir or a managed service, like Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus or Azure Monitor managed Prometheus, with Grafana on top.
@p17-601
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you control the cost of logging and observability?
K: logging cost, observability cost, reduce log volume, log retention, datadog bill, log sampling
X: Observability bills can quietly grow larger than the compute they monitor, mostly from log volume and high-cardinality metrics. I manage it deliberately.
X: Logs. Log less but better: information level for meaningful events, not every step; debug off in production; no logging of whole request and response bodies by default. Drop noise at the source or in the collector, like health check requests and chatty library logs. Sample high-volume, low-value logs, like successful request logs, keeping all warnings and errors. Use tiered retention: hot, searchable storage for 7 to 30 days, then archive to cheap object storage for compliance needs, rehydrated only when required. Convert frequent log queries into metrics, which are much cheaper to keep and query.
X: Metrics. Watch cardinality, removing labels like user or request ids. Drop unused metrics; many exporters produce hundreds of series nobody looks at.
X: Traces. Use tail-based sampling: keep errors and slow traces, sample the rest.
X: Ownership and visibility. Show each team the cost of its telemetry, by service tags, so the people generating it see it. Set quotas or alerts on daily ingestion, to catch a misconfigured deployment logging in a loop.
X: The balance: never cut audit logs or the data needed for compliance, which in a regulated domain have their own retention rules, and keep enough detail to investigate incidents. Cost cutting that leaves you blind during an outage is a false economy.
@p17-602
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you monitor message queues and consumers?
K: monitor message queue, consumer lag, queue depth alert, age of oldest message, rabbitmq monitoring, kafka lag monitoring
X: For asynchronous systems, a healthy API doesn't mean a healthy system. Messages can pile up silently while nothing shows as an error. So I monitor queues as first-class components.
X: The key signals.
X: Queue depth or consumer lag: how many messages are waiting. For RabbitMQ, ready and unacknowledged messages per queue; for Kafka, consumer group lag per partition; for SQS, approximate number of visible messages.
X: Age of the oldest message: often more meaningful than depth. A queue of 10,000 messages that's draining fast may be fine, while 20 messages stuck for an hour means something's wrong. For SQS, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage gives it directly; for others, consumers can record the time between publish and processing as a histogram.
X: Throughput: publish rate versus consume rate. If consumption is consistently lower, the backlog grows.
X: Dead-letter queue count: any message arriving there needs attention, so I alert on DLQ depth above zero, with context about which message types.
X: Consumer health: number of connected consumers, processing errors, redelivery counts, and processing duration.
X: Alerts are based on business expectations: shipment events older than five minutes, during business hours, is a problem; a nightly batch queue holding 50,000 messages at 2 AM may be normal.
X: In our platform, RabbitMQ queues and their retry and dead-letter exchanges are monitored this way, and Grafana dashboards show depth and age per queue next to the consumers' error rates.
@p17-603
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you investigate an issue with Splunk searches?
K: splunk search, spl query, splunk investigation, splunk stats timechart, search logs splunk, splunk transaction
X: Splunk is where our older platform's logs go, through Serilog, so it's often my first tool during an investigation. SPL, the Search Processing Language, is a pipeline like KQL.
X: A typical flow.
X: Narrow the scope: index, sourcetype or application, environment, and a tight time range around when the problem started. Searching everything over all time is slow and expensive.
X: Find the errors and their trend: filter by level Error and the service name, then timechart count by exception type, span five minutes. That shows when it started and whether it's one error type or many.
X: Group to find patterns: stats count by endpoint, study or site, error message, then sort descending. If all failures come from one site or one integration, that's the lead.
X: Follow one request: search by the correlation id from an error, across all services, sorted by time, to see the request's path. Our correlation id middleware puts the same id on every log line for a request, including calls into other services.
X: Compare with normal: the same query for yesterday or last week, to see whether the volume is unusual.
X: Useful commands: rex to extract a field from unstructured text, eval to compute values, transaction or stats by correlation id to group events into a request, and dedup to reduce noise.
X: Saved searches become alerts or dashboard panels. Structured logging matters a lot here: with JSON fields, searches are precise instead of fragile text matching.
@p17-604
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you use Datadog APM to find a performance problem?
K: datadog apm, datadog traces, flame graph, datadog service map, apm performance investigation
X: Our newest services send OpenTelemetry data to Datadog, and APM is where I start for performance problems.
X: The service page shows the RED metrics for each endpoint: requests, errors and latency percentiles, with deployment markers. First I check which endpoints got slower and when, and whether it matches a deployment, traffic increase or dependency change.
X: The service map shows dependencies, with latency and errors on each edge, which quickly shows whether time is spent in our service or in a downstream call, like the database, another API or the message broker.
X: Then I open traces for the slow endpoint, filtered to slow ones, like duration above the p95. The flame graph shows each span: the controller, the EF Core or SQL span with the query text, HTTP calls to other services, cache calls. The usual findings: a single slow query, many repeated queries, which is an N+1 pattern, sequential calls that could run in parallel, time waiting before the first span, which suggests thread pool or connection pool starvation, or retries hidden inside an HTTP span.
X: From a trace, logs with the same trace id are one click away, and Database Monitoring shows the query's execution plan and wait events.
X: The continuous profiler, if enabled, shows which methods use CPU and allocate memory, which helps with CPU-bound slowness that traces can't explain.
X: Then I fix, deploy, and compare the same views before and after to confirm.
@p17-605
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you detect a scheduled job that silently didn't run?
K: dead man switch, heartbeat monitoring, cron job monitoring, job did not run alert, missing job execution, watchdog job
X: Normal alerting catches things that fail loudly, like an error or an exception. A scheduled job that never starts produces no errors at all: the scheduler was stopped, a server was patched and not restarted, a trigger was misconfigured, or the job hangs forever. Nothing alerts, and the business finds out days later that no reports or reconciliations happened.
X: The fix is to alert on the absence of a signal, often called a heartbeat or dead man's switch.
X: How it works: each job, on successful completion, sends a heartbeat: a ping to a monitoring service, a metric like job_last_success_timestamp, or a row in a job history table. A separate monitor knows the expected schedule, like every hour or daily at 2 AM plus a grace period, and alerts if no heartbeat arrives in time. Tools like Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, Datadog or CloudWatch alarms with "treat missing data as breaching" support this directly.
X: Also worth monitoring: duration, since a job that usually takes five minutes but now takes three hours is a warning; output sanity, like records processed being zero when it's normally thousands; and overlap, where a run starts before the previous one finished.
X: This is a big part of what our AlertWatchDog does on the platform side: Quartz jobs that check expected events actually happened, and raise alerts when they don't. The watcher itself is monitored too, because if the watchdog stops, nothing else would notice.
@p17-606
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you write runbooks and organise on-call?
K: runbook, on call process, incident runbook, playbook operations, on call rotation, escalation policy
X: On-call works when the person paged can act quickly without needing the one expert who wrote the code. Runbooks and a sensible rotation make that possible.
X: A runbook is linked from each alert and answers: what this alert means and the user impact; how to confirm it's real, with direct links to the relevant dashboard and log queries; the likely causes, from past incidents; step-by-step mitigations, like restarting a consumer, failing over, scaling out, replaying the dead-letter queue, or switching off a feature flag; what not to do, like never purging a queue with unprocessed clinical events; and when and how to escalate. Good runbooks are short, specific and kept next to the code or in a wiki that the team actually updates after incidents.
X: Over time, repeated runbook steps become automation: a button or script that does the safe mitigation, with logging, so humans decide and tools execute.
X: On-call organisation: a rotation with a primary and secondary, usually weekly; clear escalation paths to subject matter experts and managers; a handover at the end of each shift covering open issues; and limits on load, because if someone is paged every night, the system needs fixing, not a tougher engineer. Alerts are routed by severity, so only urgent, user-impacting issues page.
X: After incidents, a blameless review leads to action items, including improving alerts and runbooks.
X: In a regulated environment, on-call actions on production are also controlled changes, recorded with who did what and why.
@p17-607
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you run a blameless post-incident review?
K: postmortem, blameless postmortem, post incident review, root cause analysis, incident retrospective, five whys
X: A post-incident review turns an outage into improvements. Blameless means we assume everyone acted reasonably with the information they had, and focus on how the system, processes and tools allowed the problem, not on who made a mistake. If people fear blame, they hide details, and you learn nothing.
X: How I run one.
X: Gather facts first: a timeline built from alerts, logs, chat messages and deployment records, covering when it started, when it was detected, by whom, the actions taken, and when it was resolved. Include the impact: which users, how long, and any data affected.
X: Analyse contributing factors, not a single root cause. Usually several things combined: a code change with an edge case, a missing test, an alert that didn't fire, a runbook that was outdated, a manual step under pressure. Techniques like the five whys help, applied to each factor. Ask what went well too, like fast rollback.
X: Look at detection and response, not just the trigger: why did it take 40 minutes to notice? Why did diagnosis take long?
X: Agree on action items, each with an owner and a date, prioritised by impact: a test, an alert, an automated safety check, a design change. Few, well-chosen actions that actually get done beat a long wish list.
X: Share the write-up widely, because other teams learn from it, and track action items to completion.
X: In our regulated context, the review also feeds the formal deviation or CAPA process when an incident affects validated functionality.
@p17-608
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you instrument a new feature before releasing it?
K: observability driven development, instrument new feature, telemetry for new feature, release monitoring plan, measure feature health
X: I treat observability as part of the feature's definition of done, not an afterthought added after the first incident.
X: Before writing code, I ask: how will we know this feature works in production, and how will we know when it doesn't? That gives a short list of signals.
X: Logs: information-level logs for key business events in the feature, with structured fields like study, site and outcome, and clear error logs with context when it fails. No personal data.
X: Metrics: a counter for the feature's main operations by outcome, a histogram for its duration, and a business metric if it has one, like the number of returns processed in the new DARM flow.
X: Traces: custom spans around important internal steps, like calculating an allocation or calling an external system, with useful attributes, so slow requests show where time goes.
X: Dashboards and alerts: a panel or a small dashboard for the feature, and alerts if failure rates exceed a threshold or the expected events stop happening.
X: Release plan: if the feature is behind a flag, I compare the signals for flag on and flag off, and check them right after rollout to each environment and each batch of users. If the numbers look wrong, the flag goes off.
X: Testing the telemetry: in integration tests or with FakeLogger and metric collectors, I check that important metrics and logs are actually emitted, because silently missing telemetry is discovered at the worst moment.
@p17-609
S: obx
D: A
T: What is continuous profiling, and when does it help?
K: continuous profiling, production profiler, cpu profiling production, pyroscope, datadog profiler, flame graph cpu
X: Traces tell you which request and which span was slow, but not which line of code inside a service burned the CPU or allocated all the memory. Continuous profiling fills that gap.
X: A profiler runs inside the application in production, all the time, with low overhead, typically a few percent, by sampling stack traces many times per second. It records where CPU time goes, which methods allocate memory, where threads wait on locks, and exceptions thrown. Data is aggregated over time and shown as flame graphs, filterable by service, version, endpoint and host.
X: Tools: Datadog Continuous Profiler, which supports .NET, Grafana Pyroscope, Azure's Application Insights Profiler, Amazon CodeGuru Profiler for some runtimes, and the OpenTelemetry profiling signal, which is maturing.
X: When it helps most. CPU is high but no endpoint looks especially slow: the profile shows the hot method, like JSON serialisation of a huge object, a regex compiled per call, or a LINQ query re-evaluated in a loop. Memory and GC pressure: allocation profiles show what's allocating, like large strings or lists built per request. Comparing versions: diffing profiles before and after a deployment shows exactly what got more expensive. Cost optimisation: shaving the top hot spots reduces instance counts.
X: Compared with taking a one-off trace with dotnet-trace, continuous profiling already has the data from when the problem happened, which matters for issues that are intermittent or can't be reproduced.
X: Profiles can contain method names and arguments' types but should never contain data values.
@p17-610
S: scx
D: A
T: An IIS-hosted .NET Framework app is stuck at 100% CPU. What do you do?
K: iis high cpu, w3wp high cpu, app pool cpu 100, dotnet framework cpu spike, debugdiag, procdump cpu
X: First, protect users, then find the cause before the evidence disappears.
X: Immediate checks: is it one server or all of them? Did it start after a deployment, a traffic spike, or a scheduled job? If it's one server behind a load balancer, I take it out of rotation so users go to healthy servers, but I don't recycle the app pool yet, because a recycle destroys the evidence.
X: Capture evidence: take two or three memory dumps of the w3wp process, about 10 to 20 seconds apart, using ProcDump with a CPU threshold trigger, or DebugDiag, or Task Manager's create dump file. Also note which requests are executing, from IIS Manager's worker processes view, or the request monitoring logs, and check Performance Monitor counters like requests queued and % time in GC.
X: Then recycle to restore service.
X: Analysis: open the dumps in DebugDiag's analysis or WinDbg with the SOS extension, and look at what the busy threads are doing across the dumps. If the same threads are in the same code each time, that's the hot spot. Typical findings: an infinite or very long loop on unexpected data, a regex with catastrophic backtracking, heavy GC caused by massive allocations, which shows as high time in GC, or lock contention with threads spinning.
X: Then fix the code, add a test with the triggering data, and add an alert on sustained CPU so we see it earlier next time.
@p17-611
S: scx
D: A
T: Latency spikes every few minutes in a regular pattern. How do you find the cause?
K: periodic latency spikes, latency every few minutes, regular spikes, cache expiry spike, gc pause spike, cron job latency
X: A regular pattern is actually good news, because regular means something scheduled or cyclic is causing it. So I look for things with the same period.
X: First, measure the period exactly, from the latency graph: every 5 minutes, every 15, on the hour? Then line it up against candidates.
X: Cache expiry: many cache entries with the same absolute expiration, like five minutes, all expiring together, so a burst of requests goes to the database at once. Fix: jittered expiration, refresh-ahead, or stampede protection like HybridCache.
X: Scheduled jobs: a Quartz job, cron job, SQL Agent job, backup, or index maintenance running on that schedule and competing for the database or CPU. Check job schedules and database activity at those times.
X: Garbage collection: large gen 2 collections when memory builds up to a threshold, visible in GC metrics, with pause times matching the spikes. Usually caused by allocation-heavy code or large object heap use.
X: Token or connection refresh: credentials, certificates or configuration refreshed periodically, blocking requests while it happens, or connection pools recycling connections at a fixed lifetime.
X: Infrastructure: health checks or autoscaling cycles, log shipping bursts, or noisy neighbours on shared hosts with their own schedules.
X: Once I have a candidate, I confirm by correlating its metric with the spikes, then change one thing and watch whether the pattern disappears. Traces of slow requests during a spike usually point straight to the waiting component.
@p17-612
S: scx
D: A
T: Database CPU jumps to 100% right after a release. What do you do?
K: database cpu 100 after release, sql server cpu spike, bad query after deployment, regression query plan, db cpu high
X: The timing makes the release the prime suspect, so I work from what changed, while keeping the system usable.
X: Find the expensive queries now: in SQL Server, sys.dm_exec_requests and sys.dm_exec_query_stats ordered by CPU, or Query Store's top resource-consuming queries for the last hour, compared with the previous period. Usually one or two queries dominate.
X: Then ask: is it a new query from the release, or an old query that changed plan? New queries: an EF Core change that now loads related data with a huge join, a missing filter, an N+1 pattern executing thousands of small queries, a LINQ expression that can't be translated well, or a new feature without the index it needs. Changed plan: a schema or statistics change in the release caused a worse plan, or a new parameter pattern.
X: Mitigation options, quickest first: if a feature flag controls the new code, switch it off. If the problem is a plan regression, Query Store can force the previous good plan. If an index is clearly missing, adding it online can be quick and low risk. If none of these work and impact is serious, roll back the application release, provided the database changes are backward compatible.
X: Then the real fix: rewrite or index the query, test with production-sized data, and add a check to the release process, like comparing query performance in a performance test environment, because slow queries usually escape when tests run on small data.
@p17-613
S: scx
D: A
T: A query was fast yesterday and is slow today, with no code change. What happened?
K: query suddenly slow, parameter sniffing, statistics out of date, plan regression, same query slow today
X: When nothing changed in the code, something changed in the data or the plan. My checklist.
X: Plan change. SQL Server compiles a plan based on the parameter values of the first execution and caches it. If the plan got recompiled, after a restart, statistics update or memory pressure, with an unusual parameter value, like a site with very few rows, the new plan, perhaps a nested loop, is terrible for typical values with many rows. That's parameter sniffing. Query Store shows the query's plans over time, so I can see the plan change and the difference in duration. Quick fix: force the good plan in Query Store. Longer fixes: OPTION RECOMPILE for queries with highly variable parameters, OPTIMIZE FOR, or restructuring the query; SQL Server 2022 also has parameter sensitive plan optimisation.
X: Statistics. After big data loads, statistics may be stale, so the optimiser underestimates row counts. Updating statistics often fixes it.
X: Data growth or skew. A table crossed a size where the plan or memory grant doesn't fit anymore, or one customer's data grew huge.
X: Blocking. The query itself is fine, but waits on locks from another process, like a new batch job. Wait stats and sys.dm_exec_requests show whether it's running or waiting.
X: Resource pressure. Other workloads on the same server, tempdb contention or I/O issues.
X: I compare actual execution plans from before and after, and look at waits, which usually reveals which of these it is.
@p17-614
S: scx
D: A
T: The cache expired and the database got overloaded. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
K: cache stampede, thundering herd, dog piling, cache expiry overload, hybridcache stampede protection, cache warmup
X: A cache stampede happens when a popular cached item expires, or the cache is emptied by a restart, and many concurrent requests all miss at once and run the same expensive database query at the same time. The database is suddenly hit with hundreds of identical queries, slows down, which makes more requests pile up. It's a classic cause of outages right after a cache restart or deployment.
X: Prevention techniques.
X: Request coalescing: only one request recomputes a given key; the others wait for that result. In .NET 9, HybridCache does this automatically for concurrent callers in the same process. Otherwise, a per-key SemaphoreSlim or Lazy task achieves it, and across servers, a short distributed lock in Redis.
X: Jittered expiration: add a random amount to each item's TTL, so items don't all expire at the same moment.
X: Refresh ahead: refresh popular items in the background before they expire, so users never see a miss. Stale-while-revalidate is a similar idea: serve the slightly old value while one request refreshes it.
X: Warm up after deployments or cache restarts, for the known hot keys, before taking full traffic.
X: Protect the database anyway: limit concurrency to expensive queries with a bulkhead, and add a circuit breaker, so even if the cache fails badly, the database survives and recovers.
X: And monitor cache hit ratio, so a sudden drop alerts us before the database falls over.
@p17-615
S: scx
D: A
T: Redis goes down in production. What happens, and what do you do?
K: redis down, cache unavailable, redis outage, redis failover, cache server down, graceful degradation cache
X: What happens depends on how we use Redis and how the app handles its failure, which is why I design for this before it happens.
X: If Redis is purely a cache, the right behaviour is graceful degradation: cache calls fail fast with a short timeout, are caught, logged and counted, and the app goes to the database instead. Users see slower responses, but everything works. The risks are that every request now waits for a long Redis timeout before falling back, so timeouts must be short and a circuit breaker should skip Redis entirely while it's down; and that the database suddenly receives the full load, so it needs headroom, or we limit concurrency on expensive queries.
X: If Redis holds state, like sessions, distributed locks, rate-limit counters or data protection keys, the impact is bigger: users logged out, locks unavailable, or rate limiting failing open or closed. Each needs a deliberate choice, like failing open for rate limits but failing safe for locks.
X: During the incident: confirm with Redis metrics and connection errors; check whether a replica failed over, in Sentinel, cluster or a managed service, since clients may need to reconnect; check memory, evictions and maxclients, since Redis often goes down from memory exhaustion; and communicate impact.
X: Afterwards: replicas with automatic failover, alerts on memory and connections, and stampede protection for when the cache comes back empty.
X: On our platform, Redis caches configuration and reference data, so the fallback is the database, with short timeouts.
@p17-616
S: scx
D: A
T: A RabbitMQ queue backlog keeps growing. What do you do?
K: rabbitmq queue growing, message backlog, queue depth increasing, consumers too slow, rabbitmq backlog, unacked messages growing
X: A growing queue means messages arrive faster than they're processed. I figure out which side changed.
X: Check consumers first. In the management UI or metrics: how many consumers are connected, and what's the consume rate? If consumers dropped to zero, they crashed, lost their connection, or a deployment stopped them. If consumers are connected but the rate is low, check unacknowledged messages: high unacked counts with a low prefetch can mean consumers are stuck on slow work, like a slow database call or a dependency timing out. Consumer logs and traces show what each message is waiting on.
X: Check for poison messages: a message that fails repeatedly and is requeued goes back to the head of the queue and blocks progress. With a proper retry and dead-letter setup, it moves aside after a few attempts; without it, it loops forever.
X: Check the producer: did the publish rate spike, like a batch import, a retry storm upstream, or a bug publishing duplicates?
X: Then act. Scale out consumers, if the work is parallelisable and the downstream dependency, often the database, can handle more load. Fix the slow dependency. Move poison messages to the dead-letter queue. Throttle the producer if possible. For large backlogs, check that the broker has enough memory and disk, because RabbitMQ blocks publishers when memory or disk alarms trigger, which spreads the problem upstream.
X: Afterwards: alerts on queue depth and the age of the oldest message, and autoscaling consumers on queue length.
@p17-617
S: scx
D: A
T: A production server's disk is full. What do you do?
K: disk full production, no space left on device, disk space alert, log files filling disk, clean disk server
X: A full disk breaks things in surprising ways: logging fails, databases stop writing, uploads fail, services can't start, and sometimes the operating system becomes unstable. So I act quickly, but carefully.
X: Find what's using space. On Windows, a tool like TreeSize or PowerShell queries for the largest folders; on Linux, df to see which volume is full and du or ncdu to find the biggest directories. Usual suspects: application logs without rotation, IIS logs that are never cleaned up, crash dumps, temp files from uploads or exports, old deployment folders kept after each release, database transaction logs or backups, and Docker images and container logs.

X: Watch out for deleted files still held open: on Linux, space isn't freed until the process closes the file, so a restart of the logging process may be needed.
X: Restore service and verify everything recovered, since some components need restarting after write failures.
X: Prevent it: log rotation and retention, cleanup jobs for temp files and old releases, logs shipped to central logging rather than kept locally, and disk usage alerts at 80 and 90 percent with time-to-full forecasting.
@p17-618
S: scx
D: A
T: A TLS certificate expired in production. How do you recover and prevent it?
K: certificate expired, ssl certificate expired production, tls cert expiry outage, certificate monitoring, auto renew certificate
X: An expired certificate causes immediate, total failures: browsers show warnings, API clients refuse to connect, and service-to-service calls fail with trust errors. Recovery is about speed.
X: Recover: identify exactly which certificate expired and where it's used. Sometimes it's not the website's certificate but an internal one, like a client certificate for a partner integration, a certificate used to sign tokens, or one on an internal API, which makes diagnosis less obvious; the error logs mention certificate validation or the remote certificate being invalid. Get a renewed certificate from the certificate authority or internal PKI, install it on every place it's used, like load balancers, IIS bindings on each server, API gateways and Kubernetes secrets, and restart or rebind where needed. Monitor expiry from outside, with synthetic checks alerting 30, 14 and 7 days ahead, including internal and client certificates. And make sure renewals reach every location automatically, not just the first one someone remembers.

D: A
T: Outbound calls start failing with DNS resolution errors. How do you troubleshoot?
K: dns resolution failure, name not resolved, no such host is known, dns errors production, dns troubleshooting
X: Errors like "No such host is known" or "Name or service not known" mean the app couldn't resolve a hostname to an IP address. It's always worth asking: is it one host or all hosts, one server or all servers, constant or intermittent?
X: Test from the same place the app runs: nslookup or dig for the hostname on the affected server or inside the container, and compare with a working machine. Check which DNS server is being used, from resolv.conf in Linux containers or the network adapter settings on Windows.
X: Common causes.

X: Network: firewall or security group changes blocking UDP and TCP port 53 to the DNS servers.
X: Caching: stale cached entries after a change, in the OS, the runtime or HttpClient's long-lived connections, where PooledConnectionLifetime helps pick up DNS changes.
X: Intermittent failures usually point to overload or one bad DNS server in a list.
@p17-620
S: scx
D: A
T: Users in another country see dates off by one day. How do you fix it?
K: date off by one day, time zone bug, utc conversion bug, date shifted timezone, datetime kind bug, visit date wrong timezone
X: "Off by one day" is almost always a time zone conversion applied where it shouldn't be, or not applied where it should.
X: Typical causes I check.
X: A date-only value stored as a date-time at midnight. A visit date of 10 March is stored as 2025-03-10T00:00 local, converted to UTC, becoming 9 March 18:30 UTC for India, and then displayed as 9 March somewhere. Or the browser parses "2025-03-10" as UTC midnight with new Date, which shows as 9 March for users west of UTC. Fix: treat date-only values as dates, DateOnly in .NET and plain date strings or a date library on the front end, with no time zone conversion at all.
X: Mixed DateTime kinds. DateTime with Kind Unspecified gets treated as local on one server and UTC on another, especially when servers in different regions have different time zones. Fix: store and transmit instants as UTC or DateTimeOffset, and convert to local only for display.
X: Wrong time zone used for business rules. A deadline like "visit window ends at end of day" must use the site's time zone, not the server's or the user's browser.
X: Daylight saving transitions, where a day has 23 or 25 hours, break code that adds 24 hours instead of one calendar day.
X: The fix includes tests with several time zones, including India, US and far-east sites, and around daylight saving changes, and running test servers in a non-UTC time zone to expose hidden assumptions.
@p17-621
S: scx
D: A
T: Customers are receiving duplicate emails or notifications. How do you investigate?
K: duplicate emails, duplicate notifications, users get two emails, notification sent twice, idempotent notifications
X: Duplicates come from something running twice, so I find what ran twice and why.
X: First, collect facts: which notifications, for which events, since when, and are the duplicates identical in content and timing? Exact duplicates seconds apart suggest retries or concurrent processing; duplicates hours apart suggest a scheduled job re-running or a replay.
X: Common causes.
X: Message redelivery: the consumer sent the email, then failed or timed out before acknowledging the message, so the broker delivered it again. At-least-once delivery means this will happen sometimes.
X: Retries: an HTTP call to the email provider timed out but actually succeeded, and the retry sent again.
X: Multiple instances: a scheduled job, like a daily reminder, running on every server instead of one, often introduced when scaling out from one server to two.
X: Duplicate events: the publishing side emitted the event twice, maybe from two code paths or a replay of the dead-letter queue.
X: Fixes. Make sending idempotent: record each notification with a unique key, like event id plus recipient plus template, in a table with a unique constraint, and skip if it already exists, before or atomically with sending. Use the email provider's idempotency key, if supported. Ensure scheduled jobs run once using clustering or a distributed lock. Make consumers deduplicate by message id.
X: I also clean up user impact, explaining and apologising if needed, and add a metric for notifications per event so duplicates are visible.

T: The same version works on one server but fails on another. How do you find the difference?
K: works on one server not another, config drift, environment difference, server inconsistency, same build different behavior
X: If the code is truly identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare systematically rather than guessing.
X: Verify it's really the same version: file versions and hashes of the deployed binaries, the build number shown by a version endpoint, and the deployment logs for that server. Partial deployments, where some files didn't copy because they were locked, are surprisingly common.

@p17-623
S: scx
D: A
T: After a front-end release, some users see a blank page or old version. Why?
K: blank page after deployment, chunkloaderror, old version after release, spa cache issue, failed to fetch dynamically imported module
X: This is usually caching combined with code splitting.
X: Single-page apps load index.html, which references bundles with hashed names, like main.a1b2c3.js, and lazy-loaded chunks. Two things go wrong after a release.
X: Stale index.html: if index.html is cached by the browser, a proxy or the CDN, users keep loading the old version, which may call APIs that changed. Fix: serve index.html with Cache-Control no-cache, so the browser revalidates every time, while hashed assets get long cache times.
X: Missing old chunks: a user has the old app open, navigates to a lazy route, and the old chunk file it references no longer exists on the server because the deployment replaced all files. The browser throws ChunkLoadError or "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module", and the route shows a blank screen. Fixes: keep previous versions' assets for a while after deploying, rather than deleting them; and in the app, catch chunk load errors and reload the page once, which picks up the new index.html.
X: Service workers can also keep serving an old version until all tabs close. Fix: a proper update flow that detects a new version and prompts the user to refresh.
X: Other causes of a blank page: a JavaScript error early in startup on certain browsers, missing runtime config, or a wrong base href on a sub-path. The browser console and front-end error tracking show which one, so I check those first.
@p17-624
S: scx
D: A
T: Refreshing a deep link in the SPA gives 404 on IIS. How do you fix it?
K: spa refresh 404 iis, angular deep link 404, react router 404 refresh, url rewrite spa, history api fallback iis
X: In a single-page app with HTML5 routing, URLs like /shipments/123 are handled by the router in the browser. Navigating within the app works because no request goes to the server. But refreshing the page, or opening a bookmarked link, sends a request for /shipments/123 to IIS, which looks for that file, doesn't find it, and returns 404.
X: The fix is a fallback rule: any request that isn't for a real file, a real folder, or an API route should return index.html, and the router then shows the right screen.

X: One detail: API calls that hit a non-existent route should still get a real 404, not index.html, which is why the API exclusion matters; otherwise, clients get HTML where they expect JSON and fail with confusing parse errors.

T: CORS errors appear right after a deployment. How do you troubleshoot?

X: CORS errors after a deployment mean the browser's preflight or response check failed, so first I find out why, from the browser's network tab, not just the console message.
X: Look at the actual request: is it the OPTIONS preflight that failed, or the real request? What status did it get? A CORS error often hides a different problem: if the API returned 500, 404 or 401 without CORS headers, the browser reports it as a CORS error. So a broken API, a wrong route after the deployment, or an authentication failure can all look like CORS.

X: The longer-term fix: environment-specific origin lists in configuration, and an automated smoke test that runs a cross-origin call after each deployment.

D: A
T: Every API call suddenly returns 401 after an identity provider change. What do you check?
K: all requests 401, jwt validation failed, signing key rotation 401, issuer mismatch, audience mismatch, 401 after keycloak change
X: When everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everyone, not individual credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate response header often includes it too, so I start there.
X: The usual causes.
X: Signing key rotation: the identity provider, like Keycloak, rotated its signing keys, and the API is validating with old keys, maybe because keys were configured statically instead of read from the JWKS endpoint, or a long cache. X: Audience mismatch: the client configuration changed, so tokens no longer include the API's audience.
X: Clock skew: a server's clock drifted, so tokens look expired or not yet valid. Check NTP.
X: Network: the API can't download metadata at all, so every validation fails.
X: Front-end side: the app's client id or scopes changed, so it gets tokens for something else, or the interceptor stopped attaching tokens.
X: I decode a failing token at a safe local tool and compare its iss, aud, kid and expiry against the API's configuration, which usually reveals the mismatch in a minute.
@p17-627
S: scx
D: A
T: A user's role was changed but they still get 403 or still have access. Why?
K: role change not applied, stale claims, permissions not updated, token claims stale, user still has access after removal
X: Usually the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed.
X: Access tokens are self-contained: when the identity provider issues a JWT, the roles inside it are fixed until it expires. If an admin adds a role, the user's existing token doesn't have it, so they get 403 until they get a new token. Worse, when a role is removed, the user keeps access until the token expires. Cookie sessions that store claims behave the same way until the session is refreshed.
X: Other places permissions get stuck: the application caches user permissions in memory or Redis, the front end caches the user's profile and hides or shows menus based on old data, or the role was changed in one system, like the identity provider, but the application maps it from its own database, which wasn't updated.
X: How I handle it. Keep access tokens short-lived, like five to fifteen minutes, so changes apply quickly through normal refresh. For removal of access, which is security-sensitive, don't wait: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens in the identity provider, and for very sensitive applications, check permissions from a server-side source per request, or use a revocation list or a security stamp checked on each request. Clear or invalidate permission caches on role changes, through events. On the front end, refresh the user profile after changes, and never rely on the front end for enforcement.
X: And explain to support teams the expected delay, so they don't raise bugs for normal behaviour.

T: A third-party API starts returning 429 Too Many Requests. What do you do?
K: third party api 429, rate limited by partner, too many requests external api, throttled by vendor, retry-after handling
X: A 429 means we're exceeding the partner's rate limit. Hammering them with retries makes it worse and can get us blocked, so I handle it on our side.
X: Immediate actions. Respect Retry-After: if the response says wait 30 seconds, wait. Make sure our retry policy isn't amplifying the problem, like three retries from each of ten instances turning one failure into many calls. Caching responses that don't change often. Batch endpoints, if the partner offers them, instead of one call per item. Spreading scheduled jobs over time instead of all at the top of the hour. Asking the partner for a higher limit if our usage is legitimate.
X: And monitoring: track 429 rates and remaining quota headers, if provided, with an alert before we hit the limit.

K: slow for some users, slow for one customer, data skew performance, tenant specific slowness, site slow only
X: When slowness affects only some users, the cause is something that differs between them, usually data size, permissions, configuration or location.

@p17-631

D: A
T: A page is fast in test but slow in production. Why?
K: slow in production fast in test, works in test slow in prod, production performance difference, test data too small
X: Test and production differ in many ways, and the most common one is data.
X: Data volume and distribution. Test databases have thousands of rows; production has millions, with skew, like one huge customer. Queries without proper indexes, or that load everything into memory, look fast in test. Checking the actual execution plan in production, or in a performance environment loaded with production-sized, anonymised data, usually reveals a scan or a bad join.
